text: 13 Introduction to male infertility SLOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Define male infertility, 2. Recognize causes of male infertility 3. Evaluate semenogram 4. Recognize investigations to evaluate male infertility and management lines Figure 1: Hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis (source : https://www2.nau.edu/~gaud/bio301/content/hpg.htm) Definition: Infertility is generally defined as the inability to achieve pregnancy after 12 months of regular, unprotected sexual intercourse, or 6 months for women over 35. This definition also include the inability to carry a pregnancy to term, including miscarriages or stillbirths. Of all sexually active couples, 12%–15% are infertile, of which a male component can be identified 50% of the time either in isolation or in combination with a female factor. Idiopathic infertility remains a common diagnosis, with approximately 25% of patients not having an identifiable cause of infertility Causes of Male Infertility Pre-testicular Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism Sperm production is deleteriously affected by a lack of testosterone (from low luteinizing hormone LH) and a lack of a stimulatory effect of Follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) on the Sertoli/germ cell complex. The most common causes of Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism include elevated prolactin, medications, illicit drugs, and pituitary damage. Idiopathic Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism ( Kallmann Syndrome) Idiopathic Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism (IHH) is a rare disorder caused by defects in gonadotropin-releasing hormone, including its action and/or release, in the setting of an otherwise normal HPG axis . While the age and severity of presentation may vary, most commonly patients present during adolescence with failure to go through puberty. Other presenting symptoms may include anosmia. In the presence of anosmia, IHH is referred to as Kallmann syndrome, which affects 1 in 8000–10,000 males. The etiology is likely genetic, and multiple genes have been identified as playing a role in pathogenesis including KAL1. Testicular Varicocele A varicocele is a dilation of the pampiniform plexus likely caused by the absence or incompetence of the venous valves of the internal spermatic vein. It is the most common surgically correctable cause of male infertility. The disruption of the heat exchange mechanism in the testis, causing hyperthermia, is the most likely mechanism. Cryptorchidism Cryptorchidism is a condition where one or both testicles fail to descend from the abdomen into the scrotum before birth. It's also known as undescended testicles. Cryptorchidism is associated with testicular hyperthermia and possible role of genetic defect in the testis. Testicular Cancer Tumors may directly disrupt spermatogenesis by mass effect, by alterations of the endocrine cascade, or by the effects of the inflammatory reaction to the tumor. Ionizing Radiation Ionizing Radiation has direct cytotoxic effect on spermatogenesis Chemotherapy Chemotherapy typically targets rapidly dividing cells and thus has profound effects on the germinal epithelium, with decline in spermatogenesis Genetic causes: It is estimated that 2%–8% of infertile men have an underlying genetic abnormality. The two potential etiologies are Y chromosome microdeletions and karyotypic abnormalities. The most common karyotypic abnormalities are Klinefelter’s (47,XXY) and chromosomal translocations. Y chromosome microdeletions occur in approximately 10% of men with azoospermia or severe oligospermia. Sertoli cell only syndrome is also associated with azoospermia. Testicular Injury Injury to the testicle can be sustained either directly or indirectly. Direct trauma can result in loss of volume of seminiferous tubules and possible obstruction from scarring is one possible cause of decreased fertility. Indirect damage to the testis may be sustained by exposure to infection or inflammation of the testis as with mumps. Infection of the testis with the mumps virus causes inflammation and swelling, which is limited by the tunica albuginea; this in turn leads to atrophy. Approximately 1.5% of postpubertal males with mumps may become infertile . Lifestyle Testicular hyperthermia, increased DNA fragmentation, and/or genetic alterations may be related to smoking, illicit drug use, or excessive heat exposure, or exposure to pesticides and heavy metals (such as lead, mercury, boron, and cadmium), and other pollutants. Antisperm antibodies Can result in Impairment of sperm motility and/or penetration Post-testicular Absence of the Vas Deferens Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens (CBA VD) is a condition strongly related to cystic fibrosis Ejaculatory dysfunction/Seminal Vesicle Dysfunction Ejaculatory duct obstruction is a common etiology of male infertility, occurring in 1%–5% of men presenting with infertility. Causes include cystic fibrosis spectrum disease, calcifications, tuberculosis and other GU infections. With chronic ejaculatory duct obstruction, the seminal vesicles may lose contractility with impaired seminal vesicle emptying during ejaculation. Nervous injury affecting ejaculation may occur at many levels and have a diverse etiology ranging from spinal cord injury to peripheral neural damage. Coital Sexual dysfunction, interference with semen deposition in vagina, lubricants may impair semen parameters. Workup: History: • sexual and medical history, including reproductive history, sexual performance, libido, prior biological children produced • family history, occupation, systemic diseases • history of significant trauma to the pelvis, testicles or head, • intake of alcohol, smoking, recreational drugs, medications, steroid abuse, • previous chemo/radiotherapy, • pubertal development, testicular descent, surgical history involving the scrotum and inguinal regions, • exposure to toxic chemicals such as pesticides, • loss of body hair, shaving frequency, anosmia (associated with Kallman syndrome), breast enlargement and galactorrhea • sexually transmitted infections (STIs), tuberculosis, mumps, scrotal infections such as epididymitis Physical examination: • signs of endocrinopathy, gynecomastia, skin, hair distribution, secondary sexual characteristics. • Examination of the penis would include a check for hypospadias, phimosis • Testicular size should be measured. In an average adult male, the testicular volume should be at least 15 ml, and the length of the testis should be at least 4 cm. • The presence or absence of the vas deferens • Any clinical abnormalities of the testicles, such as epididymal lesions, varicoceles, and hydrocele Hormonal profile: The endocrine (hormonal) lab test panel would include serum follicle- stimulating hormone (FSH), testosterone, luteinizing hormone (LH), prolactin, estradiol raised FSH level is indicative of spermatogenesis abnormalities. Semen analysis: • The WHO recommends providing a semen specimen after 2–7 days abstinence • Preferably, the specimen should be obtained in a sterile cup via masturbation either at home or in the laboratory. • The semen specimen should be evaluated within an hour of collection and stored at room or body temperature until then. • Computer-assisted semen analysis (CASA) is an automated method of determining sperm parameters which offers several advantages over manual semen analyses. The most recent WHO guidelines for semen analysis are outlined in the 6th edition of the WHO Laboratory Manual for the Examination and Processing of Human Semen (2021): • Semen Volume: >= 1.4 mL (1.3-1.5 mL) • Total Sperm Number: >=39 million per ejaculate (35-40 million) • Total Sperm Motility: >=42% (40-43%) • Progressive Sperm Motility: >=30% (29-31%) • Normal Morphology: >=4% (3.9-4%) • Sperm Vitality: >=54% (50-56%) The Nomenclature Related to the Pathological Semen Quality as Adapted from the World Health Organization Laboratory Manual for the Examination and Processing of Human Semen, WHO : • Aspermia: No ejaculate at all. • Asthe

text: 1 Basic skin lesions & skin examination & dermatologic therapies SLOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Describe the anatomy of the skin, and epidermal appendages 2. Describe the ultrastructure of the dermo-epidermal junction 3. Describe abnormalities of cutaneous histopathology 4. Describe the main functions of the skin 5. Define the vehicles of topical preparations 6. Describe cutaneous signs (initial and secondary lesions) and give examples 1. Functions of the skin: 1-Maintaining a Barrier The most obvious function of the skin is to maintain a barrier that prevents the loss of fluids, electrolytes, and other molecules from within the body, while also preventing penetration by microorganisms, toxic materials, and UV radiation . The stratum corneum is the key structure for barrier function. Protection against UV radiation occurs through several phenomena, including photon scattering in the stratum corneum and photon absorption by underlying melanin. 2- Thermoregulation Temperature regulation occurs primarily through evaporative cooling following eccrine sweating and through vasodilation and vasoconstriction. The skin and subcutaneous fat also act as insulator. Arteriovenous anastomoses, provide direct connections between arterial and venous plexuses. These anastomoses are prominent in areas exposed to maximal cooling, such as the volar surfaces of the hands and feet, lips, nose, and ears. 3-Interpersonal Communication: Beauty, Attention, and Self-Identity The skin plays an important role in interpersonal communication by conveying beauty to others, attracting attention, and contributing to the development and expression of self-identity. 4- Sensation: The skin contains nerve endings that detect sensations like touch, temperature, pain, and pressure. These sensory receptors help us perceive and react to the external environment. 5- Excretion: The skin excretes waste products, such as sweat, which contains water, salts, and small amounts of other waste products. 6- Absorption: The skin can absorb certain substances, including some medications and chemicals. 7- Vitamin D synthesis: When exposed to sunlight, the skin synthesizes vitamin D , which is essential for calcium absorption and bone health. Structure of the skin: Skin is composed of three layers: the epidermis, dermis, and subcutaneous fat (panniculus). The outermost layer, the epidermis, is composed of viable keratinocytes covered by a layer of keratin, the stratum corneum. The principal component of the dermis is the fibrillar structural protein collagen. The dermis lies on the panniculus, which is composed of lobules of lipocytes separated by collagenous septa that contain the neurovascular bundles. There is considerable regional variation in the relative thickness of these layers. The epidermis is thickest on the palms and soles, measuring approximately 1.5 mm. It is very thin on the eyelid, where it measures less than 0.1 mm. The dermis is thickest on the back, where it is 30 –40 times as thick as the overlying epidermis. The amount of subcutaneous fat is generous on the abdomen and buttocks compared with the nose and sternum, where it is extremely thin. Eccrine and apocrine glands, ducts, and pilosebaceous units constitute the skin adnexa. Figure 1: Anatomy of the skin (Andrews' Diseases of the Skin 14th Edition) Epidermis In humans, the epidermis contains four major resident populations: keratinocytes , melanocytes, Langerhans cells, and Merkel cells. The epidermis can be divided into the innermost basal layer (stratum germinativum), the malpighian or prickle layer (stratum spinosum), the granular layer (stratum granulosum), and the horny layer (stratum corneum). On the palms and soles, a pale clear to pink layer, the stratum lucidum, is noted just above the granular layer. Keratinocytes, the major population, are epithelial cells that originate from a stem cell pool situated in the basal layer; cells that leave this pool then differentiate as they migrate upward, ultimately forming the laminated stratum corneum. Under normal conditions, differentiated keratinocytes require about two weeks to exit the nucleated compartment and another two weeks to move through the stratum corneum. Melanocytes, manufacture the light -absorbing pigment melanin, which plays a major role in protecting the skin from the harmful effects of ultraviolet (UV) radiation . Langerhans cells play a critical role in antigen presentation during the regulation of immunity . Dermis Beneath the epidermis, the vascularized dermis provides structural and nutritional support. The dermis is composed of a glycosaminoglycan gel held together by a fibrous connective tissue matrix containing collagen and elastin. Vascular structures, accompanied by nerves and mast cells, course through the dermis to provide nutrition, recirculating cells, and cutaneous sensation. The dermo-epidermal junction The junction of the epidermis and dermis is formed by the basement membrane zone (BMZ). Ultrastructurally, this zone is composed of four components: the plasma membranes of the basal cells with the specialized attachment plates (hemidesmosomes); an electron-lucent zone called the lamina lucida; the lamina densa (basal lamina); and fibrous components including anchoring fibrils, dermal microfibrils, and collagen fibers in the sub-lamina densa. Type IV collagen is the major component of the basal lamina. Type VII collagen is the major component of anchoring fibrils. The two major hemidesmosomal proteins are BP230 (bullous pemphigoid antigen 1) and BP180 (bullous pemphigoid antigen 2, type XVII collagen). Laminin 332 (formerly called laminin 5) is a component of the lamina lucida/lamina densa interface. Figure 2: Structure of the epidermis (Dermatology, 5th Edition By Jean L. Bolognia, 2024) Skin appendages (Adnexa) Hairs: The hair structure divides into the hair shaft and hair follicle. The hair shaft is the portion of the hair that is visible on the outside of the skin. It is made up of cuticle cells that surround the cortex, with a central medulla present in thicker hair. The hair follicle is the primary structure for hair growth and divided into three segments: Infundibulum, Isthmus, and inferior segment. The infundibulum comprises the portion from the epidermal invagination to the level of the ductal opening of the sebaceous gland. The isthmus is the portion from the opening of the sebaceous gland to the insertion of the arrector pili muscle. The inferior segment is the growing portion of the follicle. Nails: The nail unit includes the nail plate, nail folds, and nail matrix., and nail bed. The nail matrix is the germinative zone where stem cells divide, and produce keratin for the formation of the nail. The nail plate is the visible portion of the nail that is rigid and composed of compact keratinocytes . The nail plate is curved and fits tightly into the proximal and lateral nail folds. The nail bed is the portion of the skin beneath the nail plate. Sebaceous Glands Sebaceous glands are part of the pilosebaceous unit, and there are typically multiple sebaceous glands per hair follicle. Sebaceous glands are made up of lobules and ducts. They are true exocrine holocrine glands found in all areas of the skin except for the palms, soles, and lips. The lobules are made up of sebocytes that produce sebum. These glands are pear-shaped, and their duct, the pilosebaceous canal, opens into the upper third of the hair follicle. Sweat Glands The sweat glands categorize as either eccrine and apocrine glands. Eccrine is the most common of the sweat glands, distributed all over the body except the lips and part of the external genitalia. Apocrine glands are limited to the axilla, areola, nipple, skin around the anus, and external genitalia and have an odor. name: Sexual Dysfunction
text: 9 Sexual dysfunction SLOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Define erectile dysfynction 2. Describe risk factors, pathophysiology, investigations and management lines. Definition: Erectile dysfunction (ED), formerly termed impotence, is defined as the failure to achieve or maintain a rigid penile erection suitable for satisfactory sexual intercourse Physiology of erection: The critical process in penile erection activity is the relaxation of the intracavernosal smooth muscle. This process permits increased blood flow into the corpora cavernosa, which fills with blood and compresses the emissary veins, reducing venous outflow. The paraventricular and medial preoptic nuclei of the hypothalamus control this process. Signals travel through the parasympathetic nervous system to the parasympathetic nerves of the S2-S4 sacral plexus and then to the penis via the cavernosal nerves. Nitric oxide released by the cavernous nerve terminals initiates the erectile process, while nitric oxide from endothelial cells acts to maintain it. Nitric oxide stimulates the production of cyclic guanosine monophosphate (GMP) when it enters the smooth muscle. Cyclic GMP activates protein kinase G, which opens potassium channels and closes calcium channels. Low intracellular calcium causes the intracavernosal smooth muscle tissue to relax, increasing arterial flow with simultaneous veno-occlusive activity. This results in a rigid erection with minimal blood flow into or out of the corpora once the erection is established. The phosphodiesterases (PDE) are a class of enzymes that degrade cyclic nucleotides such as cGMP and cAMP. There are over 50 isoenzymes identified to date, and PDE isoenzymes types 2, 3, 4, and 5 have been specifically located in the human corpora cavernosa. When penile phosphodiesterase degrades cyclic GMP, the corporal smooth muscle contracts again, and the process reverses. Pathology arising from any of the above processes can result in erectile dysfunction. Etiology of ED: The cause of ED is often multifactorial. It may be psychological or organic. Psychological ED may be attributed to depression, or performance anxiety Organic causes: • Aging is an essential factor contributing to ED. As patients age, cardiovascular diseases, hypertension, and other co-morbidities play an increasingly significant role in this condition. • Diabetes mellitus and metabolic syndrome can disrupt the mechanisms of erections on a molecular level • Neurological diseases (such as multiple sclerosis), • Hormonal causes (hypogonadism, thyroid), • Traumatic (e.g., pelvic fractures, spinal cord injuries), • Medications (antidepressants, antihypertensives, antipsychotics, opioids, and recreational drugs) Cardiovascular Disease and Erectile Dysfunction Cardiovascular disease is a very significant risk factor for ED. Almost 50% of men with known coronary artery disease have ED. The cavernosal arteries develop blockages from atherosclerotic plaques, resulting in vasculogenic ED and endothelial cell dysfunction Other vascular risk factors are hypertension and diabetes, lifestyle factors (such as smoking, activity level, alcohol intake, and the use of any recreational drugs Endothelial dysfunction • the endothelium is a major regulator for vascular homeostasis, producing several • signaling molecules, most notably nitric oxide, which promotes vasodilation • Endothelial dysfunction is characterized impaired nitric oxide synthesis/ degradation. Such events lead to vasoconstriction Diabetes mellitus The etiology of ED in diabetic men probably involves both vascular and neurogenic mechanisms. Endocrine disorders Hypogonadism that results in low testosterone levels adversely affects libido and erectile function. Hypothyroidism is a rare cause of ED. Medications ED is an adverse effect of some psychotropic drugs and antihypertensive agents, 5- alpha reductase inhibitors and alpha blockers. Smoking Cigarette smoking has been shown to be an independent risk factor. In studies evaluating more than 6000 men, the risk of developing ED increased by a factor of 1.5. Workup: Examination: • peripheral pulses and measure blood pressure. • Genital examination: testicular size (hypogonadism), signs of infection (such as redness and discharge in acute balanoposthitis), the presence of penile fibrosis or plaques, and phimosis (the inability to retract the foreskin). • Hair distribution, breast size (gynecomastia), • detailed neurological examination Laboratory investigations: • Hgba1c to screen for diabetes mellitus, • Lipid profile. • Testosterone level, LH and prolactin (in case of suspected hypogonadism) • TSH Further Testing Penile biothesiometry: • It involves an office screening test for penile neuropathy utilizing skin vibrational threshold sensitivity. • The process entails placing a blunt-tipped vibrating probe on the right and left shaft, as well as the glans. Patients are required to indicate when they first sense the tip vibrating, determining their threshold vibrational sensitivity. This value is compared to age-based normal standards after obtaining 5 separate readings at each site and averaging the results. • While it does not directly examine erectile nerves, it is a reasonable, safe, and cost-effective office test for penile neuropathy Nocturnal tumescence testing (NPT): • It proves valuable in distinguishing psychogenic from organic erectile dysfunction. • Testing involves measuring the frequency, tumescence (circumference changes), duration, and maximal rigidity of nocturnal erections. • Nocturnal erections require complete functioning of the neurovascular axis and typically occur during REM sleep. An average functioning man has between 3 and 6 erections a night, with a mean duration greater than 30 minutes, maximal rigidity greater than 70% at both base and tip, as well as an increase in circumference of over 3 cm at the base and 2 cm at the tip. • Men with purely psychogenic ED will typically demonstrate normal NPT tracings, while those with organic problems will show abnormal nocturnal erectile activity. Penile duplex Doppler ultrasound • This measures arterial vascular flow and checks for cavernous veno-occlusive dysfunction (venous leak). • The ultrasound is typically done by giving the patient an intracavernosal injection of a vasoactive drug, usually 20 μg of prostaglandin E1. • Following the injection, the peak systolic velocities (PSV) are measured. A normal value is > 35 cm/s, while a reading of < 25 cm/s suggests arterial insufficiency.. • Ultrasound can also demonstrate cavernous veno-occlusive dysfunction, often called "venous leak" by patients; this finding represents the failure of penile corporal rigidity despite adequate arterial inflow. Venous leak becomes evident when rapid detumescence occurs despite normal peak systolic and end- diastolic velocities (EDV > 5 cm/s Dynamic infusion cavernosometry and cavernosography Those are used for patients in whom a site-specific venous leak is suspected--usually for patients who have suffered pelvic/perineal trauma. These tests usually precede corrective vascular surgery. Treatment: Oral phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (PDE-5 inhibitors): • such as sildenafil, vardenafil, tadalafil, udenafil, avanafil, are usually the first- line treatment of ED. • competitively inhibit PDE5, decreasing the degradation of cyclic GMP via phosphodiesterase inhibition, and lead to elevated levels of cytosolic cGMP, decreased intracellular calcium which increases the relaxation of cavernosal smooth muscle and vasodilation, increased intracavernosal arterial blood flow, and penile erection. • It is important to note that PDE-5 inhibitors do not initiate the erectile response. Sexual stimulation is required to release nitric oxide from the vascular endothelium and penile nerve endings to commence the erectile process. • PDE-5 inhibitors are highly effective and have an overall success rate of up to 76%. • Should be taken on an empty st

text: No Alopecia SLOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Explain the etiology, pathogenesis, and clinical manifestations , associations, diagnosis, treatment lines of alopecia areata 2. Describe clinical features of AGA (male, female), pathogenesis, treatment lines 3. Describe clinical presentation of DLE of scalp as an example of cicatrical alopecia, treatment lines. Structure of the hair follicle: Figure 1: structure of the hair follicle Figure 2: structure of the hair follicle Figure 3: cross section of the hair follicle Hair cycle: • The timing of the phases of the hair cycle and its overall duration varies between species, between follicles in different regions of the skin in the same species . • Anagen: period of active hair growth, the duration of this phase is responsible for determining the final length of the hair. Under normal circumstances, 80–90% of hair follicles on the human scalp are in anagen at any one time. It may range from few weeks and may continue for several years. • Catagen: At the end of anagen, epithelial cell division declines and ceases, and the follicle enters an involutionary phase known as catagen. During catagen, the proximal end of the hair shaft keratinizes to form a club‐shaped structure and the lower part of the follicle involutes by apoptosis . • Telogen: The period between the completion of follicular regression and the onset of the next anagen phase is termed telogen. The club hair lies within an epithelial sac to which it is attached by tricholemmal keratin. • Exogen: The club hair lies within an epithelial sac to which it is attached by tricholemmal keratin. The club hair is eventually shed through an active process termed exogen. Figure 4 : hair cycle. • Kenogen: In the human scalp, hair follicles may remain in a state of latency, also known as kenogen, for a pro longed period after the club hair is shed. • Rate of hair growth: • Published rates of scalp hair growth in humans vary between 0.3 and 0.5 mm per day, slightly faster in adult women than men but greater in prepubertal boys than girls. • Androgen‐stimulated hair growth : • The growth of obvious facial, trunk and extremity hair in the male, and of pubic and axillary hair in both sexes, is dependent on androgens. The development of such hair at puberty is, in parallel with the rise in levels of androgen from testicular, adrenocortical and ovarian sources, which occurs in both sexes and is somewhat steeper in males. • Alopecia areata • Alopecia areata is a common, chronic, inflammatory disease that causes non‐scarring hair loss. • The incidence rate was 0.1–0.2% with a projected lifetime risk of 1.7%. • Alopecia areata occurs in all ethnic groups. • The onset of alopecia areata may occur at any age. However, in most affected individuals the first episode occurs before the age of 40, with the peak age of onset between the second and fourth decades. • The frequency of alopecia areata is probably the same in both sexes and in all races. • Alopecia areata is an autoimmune disease : • There is an increased frequency of other autoimmune diseases in patients with alopecia areata. • There is an increased frequency of organ‐specific autoantibodies in patients with alopecia areata. • Serum antibodies to hair follicle tissue also occur with increased frequency in alopecia areata . • The pathology is characterized by infiltration of hair bulbs by activated T‐lymphocytes. • In animal models of alopecia areata, the depletion of CD4 and CD8 T cells results in hair regrowth . • Alopecia areata shares genetic associations with several autoimmune diseases, particularly with genes of the major histocompatibility complex (MHC). • Pathogensis: • There is a very low or absent expression of MHC class I proteins (HLA‐A, ‐B, ‐C) in the lower part of the follicular epithelium. • Hair follicle is an immunologically privileged site. • In individuals genetically predisposed to develop alopecia areata, pro inflammatory signals such as interferon‐γ (IFN‐γ) upregulate the expression of MHC proteins and NK‐ cell‐activating ligands, leads to the collapse of immune privilege and attack by CD8+ cells. • High frequency of a positive family history in affected individuals with AA . In most reports, this ranges from 10% to 20% of cases. • • • Clinical features: • The characteristic initial lesion of alopecia areata is a circumscribed, hairless, smooth patch . • The skin within the bald patch appears normal or slightly reddened. Short, easily extractable broken hairs, known as exclamation mark hairs, are often seen at the margins of the bald patches during active phases of the disease. Figure 5: pathodynamic changes occurring in alopecia areata. • The scalp is the first affected site in most cases, but any hair bearing skin can be affected. • An intriguing feature of alopecia areata is the sparing of white hairs. • In patients with grey hair, which is an admixture of pigmented and non‐pigmented hair, the disease process appears preferentially to affect pigmented hair, so that non‐ pigmented or white hair is spared. (is probably the explanation for historical accounts of people ‘going white overnight’). • Sparing of white hair is a relative phenomenon and it is clear that the white hairs, although less susceptible to the disease, are not immune. • During the regrowth phase hairs may be non‐ or hypopigmented. • • Nail in alopecia areata • In 10–15% of cases of alopecia areata the disease also involves the nails, usually in the context of severe hair loss. Figure 6: sparing of white hair in alopecia areata. • Classically, alopecia areata causes fine stippled pitting of the nails ,but some cases show less well‐defined roughening of the nail plate (trachyonychia) or a non‐specific atrophic dystrophy. • Associated with poor prognosis. • • • Clinical types: • Patchy alopecia • Reticular type Figure 7: nail pits in alopecia areata. Pitting is highlighted by dye. • Alopecia totalis , subtotalis. • Alopecia universalis. • Ophiasis (alopecia areata of the occipital, temporal and parietal areas) • Sisaipho.( alopecia areata sparing occipital, temporal and parietal areas ) • The diffuse form of alopecia areata . • A scoring system, the severity alopecia tool (SALT) has been devised to assess the severity. • Poor prognostic signs: • Alopecia totalis. • Alopecia universalis. • Ophiasis • Long standing disease. • Early onset. • Positive family history. • Associated nail disease. • Associated auto immune diseases. • Associated diseases: • Several autoimmune diseases including thyroiditis, • Lupus erythematosus. • Vitiligo • Psoriasis. • Type 1 diabetes . • Atopic dermatitis. • • Differential diagnosis: • Causes of non cicatrical alopecia: 1. Non inflammatory tinea capitis. 2. Trichotillomania. 3. Diffuse hair loss due to systemic lupus. 4. Patchy hair loss with secondary stage syphilis. 5. Diffuse hair loss due to systemic disease. • Treatment: • In limited patchy alopecia, a potent topical steroid (e.G. Clobetasol) treatment should be continued for at least 3 months. • Intralesional steroids injection is an effective treatment in patchy alopecia areata. A depot steroid (hydrocortisone acetate 25 mg/ml or triamcinolone acetonide 5– 10 mg/ml). text: No Leukodermas SLOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Explain the etiology, pathogenesis, and clinical manifestations of vitiligo. 2. Develop the ability to make differential diagnoses, by comparing and contrasting the features of vitiligo and congenital leukodermas. Leukodermas ( hypomelanosis ) Vitiligo • Vitiligo is a common form of localized depigmentation. It is an acquired condition resulting from the progressive loss of melanocytes. It is characterized by milky‐white sharply demarcated macules. • Types: • non‐segmental forms of vitiligo (including several variants: acrofacial, mucosal, generalized, universal, mixed and rare variants of vitiligo) . • Segmental vitiligo (uni‐, bi‐, or plurisegmental). • It is stated that vitiligo affects 0.5–1% of the world’s population. • Vitiligo can begin at any age but in the majority of cases becomes apparent between the age of 20 and 30 years. • The prevalence is most probably the same in both sexes. • Vitiligo affects all races. Associated conditions: • Pathophysiology: • Histochemical studies show a lack of dopa‐positive melanocytes in the basal layer of the epidermis . • Electron microscopy studies confirm the loss of melanocytes. • Various theories have been suggested for the aetiology of vitiligo; the same mechanism may not apply to all cases. Moreover, the loss of melanocytes in vitiligo may also be the result of different pathogenetic mechanisms working together (‘convergence’ or ‘integrated’ theory). The autoimmune/autoinflammatory theory: • It is based on the clinical association of vitiligo with a number of disorders also considered to be autoimmune or autoinflammatory . • Several components of the innate immune system have been found to be associated with vitiligo . • Antibodies to normal human melanocytes have been detected using a specific immunoprecipitation assay. • A major etiological role for melanocyte‐specific cytotoxic T cells in coordinating the targeted autoimmune tissue destruction of melanocytes in progressive vitiligo . Oxidative theory: • Increased oxidative stress play an important role in in the formation of highly immunogenic neoantigens in vitiligo. Genetic theory: • A genetic factor is undoubtedly involved in vitiligo. Inheritance has been suggested to be polygenic. Approximately 30% of patients have a positive family history and vitiligo has been reported in monozygotic twins. Neural theory: • Neurogenic mechanism has been suggested whereby it has been hypothesized that a com pound released at peripheral nerve endings in the skin could have a toxic effect on melanocytes. Koebner phenomenon: • It has been defined as the development of lesions at sites of trauma to uninvolved skin of patients with cutaneous diseases . Figure 1: pathogenesis of vitiligo. Clinical types: • Non segmental type: The amelanotic macules in vitiligo are found particularly in areas of repeated friction, chonic pressure or trauma, for example the hips, dorsa of the hands/fingers, feet, elbows, knees and ankles . Figure 2: Koebner’s phenomenon. text: Page 1 of 13 No Fungal Skin Infections SLOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to Complete a clinical assessment, order the appropriate investigation(s) and justify the correct management for: 1.Tinea capitis 2. favus 3. dermatophytosis 4. candidiasis 5. pityriasis versicolor 6. onychomycosis Overview • Fungal infections, also known as mycoses, are caused by pathogenic fungi. • They can be superficial, subcutaneous, or deep, affecting skin, hair, nails, and mucosal membranes. • Superficial fungal infections are frequently encountered in dermatology practice. • Superficial fungal infections include dermatophytosis, onychomycosis, candidiasis, and pityriasis versicolor. Types • Dermatophytosis: includes tinea infections like capitis, corporis, cruris, and pedis. • Yeast Infections: Candida albicans causes yeast infections affecting mucosal and cutaneous areas, commonly leading to candidiasis. • Malassezia-Related Conditions: Malassezia furfur causes pityriasis versicolor. Transmission and Environment • Fungi thrive in warm, moist areas and spread via contact with infected people, animals, or surfaces (human-to-human, animal-to-human, and soil-to-human) Dermatophytosis • Dermatophytoses are fungal infections caused by three genera of fungi (Microsporum, Trichophyton, and Epidermophyton) that have the unique ability to invade and multiply within keratinized tissue (hair, skin, and nails). • Infections remain localized to keratinized tissues due to limited fungal virulence and host defense mechanisms. • Common types include Tinea corporis (ringworm), Tinea cruris (jock itch), Tinea pedis (athlete's foot), and Tinea ungulum (nail infection). • Characteristic red, scaly patches with raised borders and central clearing. Page 2 of 13 Tinea Corporis • Tinea corporis affects exposed skin on the trunk and limbs, sparing hair, nails, palms, soles, and groin. • Pathogens : Trichophyton (T. rubrum and T. mentagrophytes) • Clinical Presentation Lesions appear as annular with centrifugal spread, scales and pustules within the active border Associated symptoms: pruritus and burning. • Reservoirs and Resistance Hair follicles may harbor fungi, making hairier areas more resistant to treatment. Classic annular lesion with a scaly raised border and central clearing Page 3 of 13 Multiple annular and circinate lesions of various sizes on the upper back. Tinea cruris • A dermatophyte infection of the inguinal region, in particular the inner aspects of the upper thighs and crural folds. • Pathogens: Trichophyton rubrum and T. mentagrophytes, Epidermophyton floccosum • Clinical Presentation Sharply demarcated lesions with a raised, erythematous, scaly advancing border that may contain pustules or even vesicles. The disease may remain unilateral or become bilateral. Associated symptoms: pruritus and burning. Tinea manuum • A dermatophyte infection of the palm and interdigital spaces • Pathogens: T. rubrum, T. mentagrophytes, and E. floccosum. • Clinical Presentation Tinea manuum is usually non-inflammatory and often unilateral there is hyperkeratosis of the palms and digits, including within creases, that fails to respond to emollients • The differential diagnosis may include psoriasis, irritant or allergic contact Dermatitis. Page 4 of 13 Tinea manuum. A Diffuse scaling of the palm of one hand, with accentuation in the creases. Tinea pedis • A dermatophyte infection of the soles and interdigital web spaces of the feet. • Pathogens: T. rubrum, T. mentagrophytes, and E. floccosum. • Clinical Presentation There are four major clinical types of tinea pedis, moccasin , interdigital, inflammatory, and ulcerative (exacerbation of interdigital tinea pedis; ulcers and erosions in the web spaces) Maceration and scaling between the fourth and fifth toes in the interdigital form. Page 5 of 13 Erythema, scale-crust, and bullae in the inflammatory form Diffuse scaling on both feet (moccasin type) Tinea Capitis • Tinea capitis mainly affects children causing patchy hair loss, scaling, and inflammation. • Tinea capitis exhibits various forms including gray patch, black dot, and kerion. • Pathogens: Trichophyton and Microsporum species. • Clinical Presentation Black dot” tinea capitis : due to hair breakage near the scalp by T. tonsurans that causes an endothrix infection Gray patch ” tinea capitis: typically presents with dry, scaly patches of alopecia by M. audouinii which is is an ectothrix form of tinea capitis. A kerion results from advanced disease coupled with an exaggerated host response that leads to boggy, purulent plaques with abscess formation and associated alopecia with extensive lymphadenopathy Page 6 of 13 Patchy alopecia with black dots Patchy alopecia with scales Kerion Favus • Favus is the most severe form of dermatophyte hair infection • Pathogens: T. schoenleinii. • Clinical Presentation : thick, yellow crusts composed of hyphae and skin debris (“scutula”). Scarring alopecia may develop in chronic infections Page 7 of 13 • a bluish-white fluorescence by Wood’s light examination is typically seen. Favus due to Trichophyton schoenleinii. Scarring alopecia with erosions and several scutula on the occipital scalp. The latter represents masses of keratin plus fungi. Onychomycosis (Fungal Nail Infection) Pathogens: Most commonly caused by dermatophytes (e.g., Trichophyton rubrum), but also Candida species. Clinical Features: Thickened, discolored nails (yellow, white, or brown). Brittle or crumbly nails, sometimes with a foul odor. Often involves toenails more than fingernails. It is divided into three patterns based upon the point of fungal entry into the nail unit: • Distal/lateral subungual, with invasion via the hyponychium (most common • Superficial white, with direct penetration into the dorsal surface of the nail plate • Proximal subungual , with invasion under the proximal nail fold (in immunocompromised hosts) • Mixed pattern, with ≥2 of the above patterns in the same nail. Common on the chest, back, and upper arms. Pruritus is rare. Hyperpigmented variant with confluence on the lower chest. Page 11 of 13 Hypopigmented variant on the face Candidiasis • Pathogen: Candida albicans and other Candida species • Clinical Features: Erythematous,erosive, patches that are often accompanied by satellite papules and pustules. The most common sites of involvement are intertriginous zones (e.g. submammary, inguinal creases, intergluteal fold) and the scrotum, as well as the diaper area in infants. Common in skin folds (e.g., underarms, groin, under breasts). Can involve mucosal areas (oral thrush, vaginal candidiasis). text: 22 skin in systemic disease SLOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Assess a patient presenting with pruritus, recognising potential systemic causes and ordering the appropriate investigations 2. Describe cutaneous manifestations of underlying systemic disease: a) Clinical features of Vitamin A, C, K, B, b) Enumerate important cutaneous signs of Paraneoplastic phenomena c) Recognise typical nail changes seen in common dermatoses and those associated with systemic disease Pruritus Pruritus can be defined as an unpleasant sensation that elicits a desire to scratch. Pruritus is the most common skin -related symptom. It often arises from a primary cutaneous disorder but can be a manifestation of an underlying systemic disease in 15%–50% of affected individuals, especially when generalized. Non-dermatologic conditions that can lead to generalized pruritus include: • Hepatic dysfunction, Primary biliary cholangitis ( in 80% of patients, often the presenting symptom), Hepatitis C viral infection (~15%) • renal dysfunction, End-stage kidney disease on hemodialysis ( in 25-30% of patients) • thyroid dysfunction; • diabetes, • lymphoma(Hodgkin lymphoma ≤30%, Non-Hodgkin lymphoma ≤10%), myeloproliferative neoplasms (e.g. polycythemia vera 30%–50%), and chronic lymphocytic leukemia (<5%) • HIV • neuropsychiatric disorders . • Cutaneous T cell lymphoma 60%–80% overall; >90% in Sézary syndrome • Pregnancy ~20% Laboratory and radiographic evaluation in patients with pruritus of unknown etiology ❖ Basic initial evaluation • Complete blood count (CBC) with differential • Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP) • Creatinine, blood urea nitrogen (BUN) • Liver transaminases, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin • Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) • Thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) • Fasting plasma glucose • Serum ferritin, serum iron, and total iron binding capacity ❖ Possible additional evaluation • Skin biopsy • Serum total and/or allergen-specific IgE • Serum protein electrophoresis, serum immunofixation electrophoresis • Viral hepatitis panel (including hepatitis B and C viruses); • HIV testing • Parathyroid function (calcium, phosphate, parathyroid hormone levels) • Serum tryptase • Stool for ova/parasites ❖ Radiographic studies • Chest X-ray or CT scan • Abdominal and pelvic ultrasonography or CT scan • Lymph node ultrasonography • Spinal X-ray or MRI (for regional pruritus) ❖ Other investigations • Age-appropriate cancer screening Paraneoplastic phenomena Acquired hypertrichosis lanuginosa Growth of fine lanugo hairs in a generalized distribution or localized to the face. Associated with a variety of internal malignancies, most often carcinoma of the lung, colon, or breast Carcinoid syndrome Rosacea-like flushing and erythema of the head and neck and Pellagra-like dermatitis and sclerodermoid changes may develop in advanced disease Flushing associated with ~10% of mid-gut tumors (small intestine, appendix, proximal colon) with liver metastases; type III gastric and bronchial carcinoid tumors are also associated with flushing (liver metastases are not required) Paraneoplastic pemphigus Erosive disease of the mucous membranes and erythema multiforme-like, bullous pemphigoid-like or lichenoid skin lesions . Most often associated with non-Hodgkin lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic leukemia or Castleman disease. Bronchiolitis obliterans is a common complication Acanthosis nigricans Rapid onset of hyperpigmented velvety changes in multiple flexural sites (e.g. neck, axillae, groin). May also involve extensor surfaces (e.g. elbows, knees, knuckles) and, in malignancy-associated cases, lips, oral mucosa, and palms (tripe palm). Associated with adenocarcinomas (e.g. stomach, other sites within the GI or GU tracts) and often accompanied by weight loss. Dermatomyositis (adult) Diffuse scaling and pruritus of the scalp, heliotrope rash, photodistributed poikiloderma, Gottron papules of the hands, thin plaques of the elbows, knees, lateral hips/thighs (holster sign) and upper back (shawl sign), nail-fold overgrowth with dilated capillary loops . Associated with ovarian, lung, colorectal, and pancreatic carcinomas and non-Hodgkin lymphoma Acquired ichthyosis Resembles ichthyosis vulgaris; most often located on the legs. Most commonly associated with lymphoma, which typically predates the diagnosis of the ichthyosis. Cutaneous small vessel vasculitis Palpable purpura; may be widespread and/or in unusual locations . Less than 5% of patients with vasculitis have an associated malignancy, most commonly plasma cell dyscrasia, myelodysplasia, myeloproliferative or lymphoproliferative disorder, and hairy cell leukemia. IgA vasculitis in adults may be associated with solid organ malignancies Exfoliative erythroderma Widespread, diffuse, scaly erythematous skin . May be associated with cutaneous T cell lymphoma or, occasionally, with a systemic lymphoma or leukemia. Clinical features of Vitamin deficiencies: Vitamin A deficiency • Phrynoderma, which is follicular papules with central keratotic plug; favors extensor surfaces of extremities & buttocks • Generalized xerosis • Sparse, fragile hair • Night blindness, Xerophthalmia • Stunted growth Vitamin B1 (thiamin ) deficiency • Peripheral edema with possible secondary skin breakdown in “wet” beriberi • Glossitis and glossodynia • Angular cheilitis • Early – fatigue, apathy, irritability, depression, • Late – peripheral neuropathy, weakness, cardiac failure, mental alterations, growth retardation Vitamin B2 (riboflavin) deficiency • Angular cheilitis and dry fissured lips • Glossitis – pebbly appearance, then atrophic with irregular denudation of papillae • Pharyngitis • In periorificial sites (head & neck, anogenital region) painless scaly papules, ulcers, indolent fissures & seborrheic dermatitislike lesions • Conjunctivitis, Superficial keratitis, Photophobia • Anemia due to bone marrow hypoplasia • Intellectual disability in Newborns Vitamin B3 (niacin, nicotinic acid) deficiency (pellagra) • Photodistributed, well-demarcated erythema that becomes scarlet or hyperpigmented, with scale-crust; surface has shellac-like appearance • “ Casal necklace ”– well-demarcated band around the neck • Painful fissures of the palms & soles • Peri-anal & oral inflammation & erosions • Cheilitis and glossitis (atrophic, red) • Vaginitis with ulceration • Peripheral neuropathy • Late – irritability, anxiety, apathy, diarrhea, nausea, dementia Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) deficiency • Spongy gingivae with bleeding & erosions • Petechiae, ecchymoses • Follicular hyperkeratosis, especially forearms, abdomen& , legs • Corkscrew hairs (flattened & curled) with perifollicular erythema or hemorrhage • Splinter hemorrhages • Poor wound healing • Subperiosteal hemorrhage with “pseudoparalysis,” especially in children • Arthralgias, joint swelling, edema • Loose teeth • Weakness, malaise, depression, Vasomotor instability Vitamin K deficiency: (K1:phytonadione, source :diet; K2: menaquinone, source: gut bacteria ( • Petechiae, purpura, ecchymoses, • mucosal bleeding • if severe hypoprothrombinemia, extensive hemorrhage at any body site • Hemorrhagic disease of the newborn – infants not given vitamin K at birth plus inadequate diet or mother on medications which inhibit vitamin K function Nail changes associated with systemic disease Clubbing Clubbing is caused by enlargement of the soft tissue of the distal digit, leading to a bulbous appearance. The nail plate is enlarged and excessively curved, with widening of the angle between the proximal nail fold and the nail plate to greater than 180° (Lovibond’s sign). In hypertrophic osteoarthropathy, clubbing is associated with hypertrophy of the extremities and painful pseudoinflammatory joint disease. text: 21 Cutaneous manifestations of HIV SLOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Recognize the cutaneous manifestations of the different stages of HIV There are two types of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), HIV-1 and the less common HIV-2. Both are enveloped, single-stranded RNA lentiviruses in the Retroviridae family. Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infects human Th cells, leading to a progressive immunodeficiency disease, and causes acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). Cutaneous manifestations are prominent, affecting up to 90% of HIV-infected persons. In a person living with HIV , acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) is defined by a CD4+ cell count of <200/mm3 or <14% CD4+ T cells and/or the presence of an AIDS-defining condition. Figure 1: Replication of HIV within CD4+ lymphocyte and target sites of antiretroviral drugs (Dermatology, 5th Edition By Jean L. Bolognia, 2024) WHO clinical staging of HIV/AIDS in the setting of confirmed HIV infection: Clinical stage 1 – asymptomatic; immunologic correlate: ≥500 CD4+ cells/mm3 •Asymptomatic •Persistent generalized lymphadenopathy Clinical stage 2 – mild; immunologic correlate: 350–499 CD4+ cells/mm3 •Herpes zoster •Fungal nail infection •Pruritic papular eruptions •Angular cheilitis •Recurrent oral ulcerations •Recurrent/chronic upper respiratory tract infections (sinusitis, otitis media/ otorrhea, tonsillitis, pharyngitis) •Seborrheic dermatitis •Moderate unexplained weight loss (<10% of body weight) Clinical stage 3 – advanced; immunologic correlate: 200–349 CD4+ cells/mm3 •Persistent oral candidiasis •Oral hairy leukoplakia •Acute necrotizing ulcerative stomatitis, gingivitis, or periodontitis •Unexplained chronic diarrhea (>1 month in adults, >2 weeks in children) •Unexplained persistent fever (≥37.6°C intermittent or constant, for >1 month) •Pulmonary tuberculosis (current) •Unexplained anemia (<8g/dL), neutropenia (<0.5 × 109/L) or chronic thrombocytopenia (<50 × 109/L) •Unexplained severe weight loss (>10% of body weight) •Severe bacterial infections such as pneumonia, empyema, pyomyositis, bone or joint infection, meningitis, bacteremia Clinical stage 4 – severe/AIDS-defining conditions; immunologic correlate*: <200 CD4+ cells/mm3 •Chronic herpes simplex infection (orolabial, genital, or anorectal of >1 month’s duration or visceral at any site) •Kaposi sarcoma •Extrapulmonary cryptococcosis including meningitis •Disseminated endemic mycosis (coccidioidomycosis or histoplasmosis) •Disseminated non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection •Unexplained severe wasting, stunting or severe malnutrition not responding to standard therapy (HIV wasting syndrome) •Cytomegalovirus infection (retinitis or infection of other organs; onset at age >1 month) •HIV encephalopathy •Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy •Extrapulmonary tuberculosis •Candidiasis of the esophagus, trachea, bronchi, or lungs •Pneumocystis pneumonia •Central nervous system toxoplasmosis (onset at age >1 month) •Chronic cryptosporidiosis (with diarrhea) •Chronic isosporiasis •Symptomatic HIV-associated nephropathy or symptomatic HIV-associated cardiomyopathy •Cerebral or B cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma, or other HIV-associated solid tumor •Atypical disseminated leishmaniasis •Recurrent severe bacterial pneumonia •Recurrent non-typhoidal Salmonella bacteremia •Invasive cervical carcinoma Primary HIV exanthem (acute retroviral syndrome) Primary HIV infection refers to the initial disease phase, when HIV-1 RNA, DNA, and/or p24 antigen are present in the plasma prior to the development of HIV-1 antibodies. Initially, up to 80% of patients develop an “acute retroviral syndrome” resembling influenza or infectious mononucleosis. Symptoms develop 2–6 weeks after HIV exposure and often include fever, headache, myalgia/arthralgia, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, and night sweats. A morbilliform exanthem also occurs in 40%– 80% of patients; it lasts 4–5 days and is typically generalized, with the most prominent involvement on the face and trunk. Oral and genital ulcers are occasionally present. Symptoms are self-limited and resolve in a few days to weeks, with a median duration of 14 days. The initial phase of rapid HIV-1 replication causes a temporary fall in CD4+ cell counts HIV-related infectious skin conditions As immunity wanes, the frequency of Herpes Simplex Virus recurrences increases and lesions take longer to heal, potentially evolving into chronic, extensive, deep, and painful ulcers that favor the perianal region, genitalia, and tongue In people living with HIV , varicella tends to have new lesion formation over a longer period of time, a higher lesion count, and (particularly in adults) complications such as pneumonitis, hepatitis, and encephalitis. Lesions persist as slowly healing ulcers. Molluscum contagiosum (MC) commonly occurs and tends to be more persistent in individuals with significantly reduced CD4+ T cell counts. In addition to the typical presentation of small umbilicated papules , people living with HIV can develop larger (>1cm), coalescent, verrucous, and widespread lesions The prevalence of human papilloma virus (HPV) infection is higher in people living with HIV than in the general population and correlates with decreasing CD4+ T cell counts. People living with HIV have reduced HPV clearance, more treatment-resistant mucocutaneous lesions, and accelerated development of HPV-associated carcinoma. Skin lesions are often multiple, coalescent, and extensive Oral hairy leukoplakia (OHL) results from Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) infection of the oral mucosa and typically presents as hyperkeratotic, corrugated white plaques with hair-like projections on the lateral aspect of the tongue Reactivation of cytomegalovirus (CMV) is associated with CD4+ T cell counts that are <100/mm3, and it remains a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in patients with AIDS. Retinitis, esophagitis, and colitis represent common clinical manifestations, and mucosal ulcers may occur in the setting of disseminated disease. Cutaneous presentations are uncommon People living with HIV are at increased risk for the development of recurrent and potentially severe cutaneous bacterial infections, which can be localized or widespread and sometimes have unusual clinical appearances. A diverse clinical spectrum of tuberculous and non-tuberculous mycobacterial skin infections can develop in people living with HIV Rates of syphilis have risen over the past decade. In addition to classic papulosquamous lesions of secondary syphilis, people with HIV disease may present with lues maligna, also known as malignant or ulceronodular syphilis, which is a severe form of secondary Syphilis. Candidiasis is the most common fungal disease in those living with HIV , and its incidence and severity are both increased in the setting of lower CD4+ T cell counts. Oropharyngeal candidiasis is often the first clinical manifestation of HIV disease. Additional presentations include angular cheilitis, chronic paronychia, and onychodystrophy, as well as intertriginous, refractory vaginal, esophageal, and disseminated candidiasis. Individuals with HIV disease are predisposed to the development of disseminated cryptococcosis and dimorphic fungal infections, including histoplasmosis, blastomycosis, coccidioidomycosis, paracoccidioidomycosis, talaromycosis, emergomycosis, and sporotrichosis. Cryptococcus neoformans is an encapsulated yeast that is found worldwide in bird droppings and contaminated soil. Patients with CD4+ T cell counts <100/mm3 are particularly susceptible, and pulmonary or central nervous system disease may be the initial presentation of AIDS. Cutaneous lesions occur in 10%–20% of patients with disseminated cryptococcosis and often appear as molluscum contagiosum-like. name: leprosy
text: No Leprosy SLOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Describe Classification, clinical features of main types. 2. Histopathology, reactional states, management. Leprosy: Hansen’s disease • About 4 million people have, or are disabled by, leprosy. • Leprosy can occur at all ages but there is a peak in the teens and early twenties. • Leprosy occurs equally in both sexes. Pathophysiology: • Living in a leprosy endemic area, age, sex and household con tact predispose to acquiring leprosy . • Bacille Calmette–Guérin (BCG) vaccination protects against leprosy. • Nasal discharges from untreated LL patients, who are often undiagnosed for several years, are the main source of infection in the community. • In patients with the tuberculoid types of leprosy, M. leprae remains within the skin and nerve compartments and these patients are probably never infectious. • Infection probably also occurs through the nose. Mycobacterium leprae is inhaled, multiplies on the inferior turbinates and has a brief bacteraemic phase before binding to Schwann cells and macrophages. • The skin is unimportant in leprosy transmission. Bacilli are rarely found in the epidermis and are only excreted by untreated LL patients. • Mycobacterium leprae: • Limited growth has been achieved in nine‐banded armadillo. • Mycobacterium leprae grows at 30–33°C, with a doubling time of 12 days. • Remains viable in the environment for up to 10 days. • Mycobacterium leprae has a complex antigenic cell wall composed of lipids, carbohydrates and proteins. The organism also synthesizes a species‐specific lipid, phenolic glycolipid (PGL). • The pathogenesis and thus the clinical features, reflect four principal causes of tissue damage: • The degree to which cell‐mediated immunity (CMI) is expressed. • LL represents a failure of CMI specifically towards M. leprae with resultant bacillary multiplication. The absence of activated lymphocytes and macrophages means that nerve dam age is slow and gradual in onset. • In tuberculoid leprosy, CMI is strongly expressed, so that the infection is restricted to one or a few skin sites and peripheral nerves. Lymphocytic infiltration rapidly causes nerve damage. • Between them lies the borderline forms of disease, with the extent of disease reflecting the balance between CMI and bacillary load. • The extent of bacillary spread and multiplication: • In LL, haematogenous spread of bacilli occurs to cool, superficial sites, including eyes, upper respiratory mucosa, testes, small muscles and bones of hands, feet and face, as well as peripheral nerves and skin. • In tuberculoid leprosy, bacillary multiplication is restricted to a few sites and bacilli are not readily found. • The appearance of tissue‐damaging immunological complications/ lepra reactions : • Borderline patients (borderline tuberculoid (BT); borderline borderline (BB); BL) are immunologically unstable and at risk of developing immune‐mediated reactions. • Type 1 (reversal) reactions are delayed hypersen sitivity reactions caused by increased recognition of M. leprae antigens in skin and nerve sites. • Type 2 reactions, erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL), are due in part to immune complex deposition and occur in BL and LL patients who produce anti bodies and have a large antigen load. • The development of nerve damage and its complications: • Nerve damage occurs in two settings, in skin lesions and in peripheral nerve trunks. • In skin lesions, nerve damage cause local sensory loss and loss of sweating within the area of the skin lesion. • In Peripheral nerve trunks , small increase in nerve diameter leads to raised intraneural pressure, with consequent neural compression and ischaemia. With resulting dermatomal sensory loss and dysfunction of muscles supplied by that peripheral nerve. • Nerve damage: • leads to anaesthesia, muscular weakness and contracture, and autonomic dysfunction. • These permit trauma, bruising, burns, cuts and, especially, tissue necrosis from pro longed, inappropriate or repetitive trauma, which in turn lead to ulceration, secondary cellulitis and osteomyelitis and loss of tis sue, so that deformity is added to disability. • Mycobacterium leprae: • Intracellular pleomorphic non sporing non motile acid fast pathogenic aerobic bacilli. • It is gram positive by gram staining. • Has a predilection for neural tissue. • Bacilli probably enter nerves via endoneural blood vessels . • The target cell being the schwann cell. • In the dermis, the type and degree of cellular infiltrate reflects the degree of CMI. • Figure 1: mycobacterium leprae. • • Figure 2: mycobacterium leprae. • • • Clinical picture: • Leprosy is a chronic disease with a long incubation period. An average incubation time of 2–5 years has been calculated for tuberculoid cases, and 8–12 years for lepromatous cases. • The commonest early lesion is an area of numbness on the skin, or a visible skin lesion. • The classic early skin lesion, which is most commonly found on the face, extensor surface of the limbs, buttocks or trunk. Scalp, axillae, groins and lumbar skin tend to be spared. • Indeterminate lesions consist of one or more slightly hypopigmented or erythematous macules, a few centimetres in diameter, with poorly defined margins. • Patients frequently present with signs of nerve damage: weakness or anaesthesia due to a peripheral nerve lesion, or a blister, burn or ulcer in an anaesthetic hand or foot. Figure 3: mechanisms of tissue damage in leprosy. Figure 4: indeterminate leprosy. Tuberculoid leprosy: • Only nerves and skin show clinical evidence of disease; lesions are few, often solitary. • The typical lesion is a plaque that is conspicuous, erythematous, copper coloured or purple, with raised and clear‐cut edges sloping towards a flattened and hypopigmented centre. • Dark skins may not show the erythema. The surface is dry, hairless and insensitive, and sometimes scaly. • Thickened sensory nerve may be palpated or a thickened nerve trunk may be felt in the vicinity, for example a thickened ulnar nerve if the lesion is on the arm. • • Lepromatous leprosy: • The first clinical manifestations are usually dermal (because early nerve involvement is usually asymptomatic), but they may go unnoticed by the patient, who often complains of other early symptoms; these include nasal symptoms of stuffiness, discharge and epistaxis. • Signs comprise macules, diffuse papules, infiltration or nodules, or all four. • Macules are small, multiple, erythematous or faintly hypopigmented, with vague edges and shiny surface. Figure 5: tuberculoid leprosy. • • Figure 6: lepromatous leprosy. Lepromatous leprosy: • Papules and nodules usually have normal skin colour but sometimes are erythematous ,with a bilaterally symmetrical distribution on face, arms, legs and buttocks, but may be anywhere apart from hairy scalp, axillae, groins and perineum (i.e. regions of skin with the highest temperature). • Hair growth and sensation are not initially impaired over the lesions. Figure 7: lepromatous leprosy. • Lesions of oral mucosa occur as papules on lips and nodules on palate (which may perforate), uvula, tongue and gums . • The nasal mucosa is hyperaemic or ulcerated and bleeds easily; epistaxis is common. • Nerve affection causing numbness and anaesthesia on the dorsal surfaces of hands and feet, and later on extensor surfaces of arms and legs, and finally over the trunk. • Infiltration of corneal nerves causes anaesthesia, which predisposes to injury, infection and blindness . • If the patient remains untreated the lines of the forehead become deeper as the skin thickens (leonine facies), eyebrows and eyelashes become thinned or lost (madarosis), ear lobes are thickened, the nose becomes misshapen, and may collapse due to septal perforation and loss of the anterior nasal spine, the voice becomes hoarse . • • Figure 8: lepromatous leprosy. • • Figure 9: lepromatous leprosy with dactylitis and lepromatous nodules. • • Figure 10:

SLOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to Describe pathogenesis, clinical features, clinical types, histopathologic changes, treatment lines. Lichen planus • Lichen planus (LP), the most typical and best characterized lichenoid dematosis, is an idiopathic inflammatory skin disease affecting the skin and mucosal membranes. • Its prevalence is approximately 0.5% of the population. • Lichen planus is thought to be a T‐cell‐mediated autoimmune disease, possibly targeting the basal keratinocytes, which can be triggered by a variety of situations, including viruses, drugs and contact allergens. Pathogensis: • In LP lesions, T cells, both CD4+ and CD8+, accumulate in the dermis, whereas CD8+ T cells infiltrate the epidermis. It has been proposed that CD8+ cytotoxic T cells recognize an antigen (currently unknown) associated with major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I on lesional keratinocytes, and lyse them. • Keratinocyte derived cytokines may up‐regulate the expression of cell surface adhesion molecules on, and migration by, T cells .CD1a+ Langerhans cells and factor XIIIa+ cells are increased in LP and may be involved in antigen presentation to T cells. • Several studies suggested a role for HCV, hepatitis B virus (HBV), human herpesvirus 6 (HHV‐6) and HHV‐7 and varicella zoster virus. • An association with HLA‐A3 and HLA‐5 has been documented. • The list of drugs causing LP and LP‐like eruptions has grown steadily and includes several classes, including antimicrobials, antihypertensives, antimalarials, antidepressants, anticonvulsants, diuretics, metals, non‐ steroidal anti‐inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and more recently imatinib, intravenous immunoglobulin, etanercept and adalimumab. • Clinical picture: • Shiny, polygonal, 1–3 mm diameter papules with a red to violet color sometimes with central umbilication . • White lines can be seen on the surface of the lesions, known as Wickham’s striae. • Papules can be isolated or grouped, in a linear or annular distribution. Typically, a greyish brown pig mentation can be observed in lesions that have resolved due to deposition of melanin in the superficial dermis. • LP can affect any part of the body surface, but is most often seen on the volar aspect of the wrists , the lumbar region and around the ankles. • Co‐localization of LP and vitiligo has been reported. • Pruritus is a fairly consistent feature in LP and ranges from occasional mild irritation to more or less continuous, severe itching, which interferes with sleep and makes life almost intolerable. • Annular lesions are especially common on the penis. • • Figure 1: classical lichen planus. • • Annular lichen planus: • Present as persistent, asymptomatic erythematous macules and round, annular patches with a red‐brownish border and central hypopigmentation, mostly dis tributed on the groin and flanks, in children and adolescents. Figure 2 : lichen planus, an annular lesion on the penile shaft. • Lichen planopilaris: • A variant in which groups of ‘spiny’ lesions resembling keratosis pilaris develop around hair follicles are likely to lead to a scarring alopecia . • The so‐called Graham Little–Piccardi–Lassueur syndrome comprises the triad of multifocal scalp cicatricial alopecia, non‐scarring alopecia of the axillae and/or groin, and keratotic lichenoid follicular papules. Figure 3: annular lichen planus. • Figure 4: cicatrical alopecia due to lichen planus of the scalp. • • Figure 5: lichen planopilaris. • Hypertrophic LP: • The ankles and shins are the commonest sites for hypertrophic lesions. • Multiple cutaneous horns overlying hypertrophic LP , as are keratoacanthoma and malignant transformation arising in hypertrophic LP , as well as metastatic squamous cell cancer are recorded. • Figure 6: hypertrophic lichen planus. • Guttate lichen planus: • Lesions are widely scattered and remain discrete, may be all small (1–2 mm across), or larger (up to 1 cm), and individual lesions rarely become chronic . • Figure 7: guttate lichen planus. • Actinic lichen planus: • Mostly in children or young adults with dark skin. • well‐defined annular or discoid patches, which have a deeply hyperpigmented center surrounded by a striking hypopigmented zone. • Sunlight exposure may play a role. • Palmoplantar LP: • Palms and soles are affected, the lesions tend to be firm and rough with a yellowish hue. • Figure 8: palmoplantar lichen planus. • Lichen planus pigmentosus: • The macular hyperpigmentation involves chiefly the face, neck and upper limbs, although it can be more widespread, and varies from slate grey to brownish black. • It is mostly diffuse, but reticular, blotchy and perifollicular forms can be present. • • Rare types : • A rare, erosive, flexural variant of LP has been described. • Linear LP occurring on Blashko’s lines . Figure 9: lichen planus pigmentosus . • Mucosal LP: • Mucous membrane lesions are very common, occurring in 30–70% of cases. Mucosal lesions occurring alone without skin lesions account for about 15% of all cases. • Distinct clinical subtypes such as reticular, atrophic, hypertrophic and erosive forms are well recognized, and more than one type may be present. • Diabetes is a possible associated disease of oral LP , and candidiasis may coexist with LP in some patients. • Reticular LP: • White streaks, often forming a lacework, on the buccal mucosa are highly characteristic. • They may be seen on the inner surface of the cheeks, on the gum margins or on the lips. • Figure 10: reticular oral lichen planus. • Tongue in LP: • On the tongue, the lesions are usually in the form of fixed, white plaques, often slightly depressed below the surrounding normal mucous membrane, especially on the upper surface and edges. • Figure 11: lichen planus of the tongue. • Erosive LP: • Presents on the gingiva and buccal mucosa. • • Ulcerative mucosal LP: • Ulcerative lesions in the mouth are uncommon, but may be the site of epitheliomatous transformation. • There may be striking pigmentation of oral LP in darkly pigmented races. Figure 12: erosive oral lichen planus. • • • Genital lichen planus: • Genital lesions, which are usually characteristic, may be present on the penile shaft, glans penis, prepuce or scrotum. • In females, it may present in the vulva, as well‐demarcated erosions/erythematous areas at the vaginal introitus, the presence of a hyperkeratotic border to lesions and/or Wickham’s striae in the surrounding skin, symptoms of pain/burning, with or without scarring. Figure 13: oral pigmentation and gingivitis in oral lichen planus. • • • Bullous lichen planus: • In bullous LP , blisters arise only on or near the lesions of LP . • Histologically, there is subepidermal bulla formation with typical changes of LP . Figure 14: genital lichen planus in a female patient. • Lichen planus pemphigoides: • In LP pemphigoides the LP tends to be acute and generalized and is followed by the sudden appearance of large bullae on both involved and uninvolved skin. • In LP pemphigoides, the histology shows a subepidermal bulla with no evidence of associated LP . • • • Nail lichen planus: • Nail involvement occurs in up to 10% of cases. • Fingernails are more frequently affected than toenails. Figure 15: lichen planus pemphigoides. • The most common changes are exaggeration of the longitudinal lines and linear depressions due to slight thinning of the nail plate. • Adhesion between the epidermis of the dorsal nail fold and the nail bed may cause partial destruction of the nail (pterygium unguis). • LP of the nail bed may give rise to longitudinal melanonychia, hyperpigmentation, subungual hyperkeratosis or onycholysis. • • Figure 16: nail lichen planus. • Associations: • Idiopathic LP has been reported in association with diseases of altered or disturbed immunity, including : • Diabetes mellitus. • HCV, HBV. • Ulcerative Colitis • Alopecia Areata. • Vitiligo. • Dermatomyositis . • Morphoea . • Lichen Scl

Overview Common Bacterial Pathogens • Staphylococcus aureus, Group A Streptococcus, and Corynebacterium minutissimum Infection Classification • Skin infections are classified into superficial types like impetigo and superficial folliculitis, and deeper infections such as boils, cellulitis and erysipelas. Risk Factors • Poor hygiene, warm climates, and immunosuppression increase susceptibility to bacterial skin infections. Imptigo Definition & Pathogenesis • Superficial epidermal infection. • Common pathogens: Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes. • Two types: Non-bullous (most common), Bullous (toxin-mediated). • Highly contagious. • Usually resolves without scarring if untreated Page 2 of 15 Non bullous Impetigo. Superficial erosions with honey-colored crusting. Bullous impetigo. Multiple superficial erosions with collarettes on the lateral aspect of the trunk Non-bullous Impetigo • 70% of all cases of impetigo • Children most often affected • Honey-colored crusted erosions, Face (around the nose and mouth) and extremities. • Complications: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. Honey-colored Page 3 of 15 crusts on the chin of a child with non-bullous impetigo Multiple small superficial erosions with crusting around the nares and on the chin in association with folliculitis in an adult. Bullous Impetigo • Less common • Often occurs in neonates (see Ch. 34) and children • Flaccid bullae, rupture leaving a collarette of scale, but no thick crust; usually little surrounding erythema. • Face, trunk, buttocks, perineum, axillae, and extremities • Complications: staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome Page 4 of 15 Superficial round to oval erosions with central thin crusting and a peripheral collarette due to bullous impetigo in the axilla and on the neck. Note the small intact vesicles on the upper anterior neck Diagnosis & Treatment Diagnosis: mainly clinical; cultures if outbreak or resistance. Treatment: 1- Cleansing the affected area and removing crusts 2- Topical mupirocin or fusidic acid for localized lesions. 3- Systemic antibiotics for extensive or resistant cases (Dicloxacillin, 500 mg PO four times a day; First generation cephalosporin cephalexin, 250–500 mg PO three or four times a day). Supportive care: hygiene, nutrition. Page 5 of 15 Impetigo Ecthyma (Ulcerative impetigo) Definition and Cause Ecthyma is a deeper form of impetigo caused by Group A beta -hemolytic Streptococci and Staphylococcus aureus. Clinical Presentation Ecthyma presents as painful punched-out ulcers with thick brown-black crusts, often on lower extremities. Diagnosis and Treatment Diagnosis is clinical; Culture tests guide therapy in severe cases. Treatment: oral antibiotics ((e.g., dicloxacillin, cephalexin). Ulceration with hemorrhagic crust on the wrist and leg Page 6 of 15 Page 7 of 15 Folliculitis • Definition and Causes Folliculitis is inflammation of hair follicles commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus bacteria. • Types and Symptoms Superficial folliculitis (Bockhart’s impetigo) Deep: Furuncles, carbuncles. • Risk Factors : Shaving, occlusion, immunosuppression. • Diagnosis: Clinical, Gram staining and bacterial cultures in severe, recurrent, or treatment-resistant cases. Folliculitis Page 8 of 15 Superficial Folliculitis • Small (1–4 mm) pustules or crusted papules on an erythematous base. • The lesions are frequently clustered and heal without scarring. • Treatment: 1. Antibacterial washes. 2. Topical antibiotics such as mupirocin or clindamycin for 7–10 days to treat localized lesions. 3. When staphylococcal folliculitis is widespread or recurrent, oral β-lactam antibiotics (e.g. a β- lactamase-resistant penicillin or first -generation cephalosporin), tetracyclines, trimethoprim – sulfamethoxazole (TMP -SMZ), macrolides, or linezolid (depending on local resistance patterns). Sites prone to friction or minor trauma, such as the area under a belt. • Furuncles begin as firm, tender, red nodules that progressively enlarge, becoming painful and fluctuant, rupture results in decreased pain. Page 10 of 15 Furuncles. Fluctuant erythematous nodules with a central pustule on the ankle (A) and finger (B). Carbuncles • are collections of furuncles that extend deep into the subcutaneous tissue. The surface usually displays multiple draining sinus tracts and occasionally ulcerates. • They usually occur in areas with thicker skin (e.g. nape of neck, back, thigh). • Systemic symptoms are often present. • Heal with scarring Page 11 of 15 Carbuncles Treatment of deep folliculitis • For simple furuncles, warm compresses may promote maturation, drainage, and resolution. Larger or • Deeper fluctuant lesions typically require incision and drainage. • Systemic antibiotic therapy is recommended in the following situations: (1) Furuncles around the nose, in the external auditory canal, or in other locations where drainage is difficult (e.g. elsewhere on the face, hands, genitalia); (2) Severe or extensive disease (e.g. multiple sites); (3) lesions with surrounding cellulitis/phlebitis or associated with signs/symptoms of systemic illness (4) lesions not responding to local care Patients with concerning comorbidities or immunosuppression Sycosis barbae Definition and Symptoms Sycosis barbae, a type of deep folliculitis in the beard area, appears as large erythematous papules, often with a central pustule and sometimes coalescing to form plaques studded with pustules and crusts Causes and Aggravation The condition is aggravated by shaving and involves Staphylococcus aureus infection. Diagnosis and Treatment Diagnosis is clinical; treatment involves oral antibiotics and hygiene management. Prevention and Care Avoid shaving during infection and maintain good hygiene to prevent recurrence.
