text: Page 1 of 13 No Urticaria SLOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Describe wheal 2. Recognize causes and immunopathogenesis of urticaria, urticarial vasculitis 3. Describe the clinical picture 4. Recognize types of physical urticaria 5. Define management lines of acute and chronic urticaria 6. Define hereditary Angioedema, types, management lines Urticaria A common disease that may present with wheals, angio-oedema or both Page 2 of 13 Urticaria Wheal • A transient, well -demarcated, superficial erythematous or pale swellings of the dermis, which are usually very itchy and are associated with a surrounding red flare initially. • Lesions may be a few millimeters in diameter or as large as a hand, and the number can vary from a few to numerous. Page 3 of 13 • The hallmark of wheals is that individual lesions come and go rapidly (less than 24 hours) Wheal Angioedema • Swellings affect the deeper dermal, subcutaneous and submucosal tissues. • They are usually painful rather than itchy, poorly defined, and pale or normal in colour Page 4 of 13 Angioedema Pathogenesis • The mast cell is the primary effector cell of urticaria • Mast cell granules contain preformed mediators of inflammation, the most important of which is histamine Page 5 of 13 Clinical classification • According to its duration as acute or chronic 1. Acute urticaria: urticaria present daily or almost daily for less than 6 weeks 2. Chronic urticaria: urticaria occurs continuously (at least twice a week off treatment) for longer than 6 weeks • According to the role of definite triggers as inducible or spontaneous Chronic urticaria is classified as 1. chronic spontaneous urticaria. 2. chronic inducible urticaria. Chronic spontaneous urticaria: • 1. CSU with known cause • 2. CSU with unknown cause. Urticaria Page 6 of 13 Causes of acute urticaria Page 7 of 13 Causes of chronic urticaria Page 8 of 13 Inducible urticarias: • Inducible urticaria is characterized by definite and specific triggers of the development of wheals, angioedema, or both. • Wheals occur within minutes of provocation and generally resolve within 2 hours, • A few physical urticarias (e.g. delayed pressure urticaria, delayed dermographism) develop after a delay of several hours and persist for 24 hours or longer. • Dermographism Page 9 of 13 Delayed pressure urticaria Page 10 of 13 Urticarial Vasculitis A clinicopathologic entity in which lesions resemble urticaria clinically, but 1-Last longer than 24 hours 2-Painful & burning sensation as well as pruritus 3-leave residual, purpura. 4-Associated with SLE, HCV Urticarial vasculitis Management of acute urticaria • Assess and remove triggers: Identify any recent exposures (foods, drugs, infections, temperature changes, stress) and advise avoidance • First-line: Start a second -generation (non -sedating) H1 -antihistamine (e.g. cetirizine, levocetirizine, loratadine, fexofenadine) at standard dose If inadequate control: 1-Increase antihistamine (up-dosing) gradually. Doses up to 2–4× 2-If a particular H1-antihistamine is ineffective, switch to or combine with a different second-generation agent. 3- Add adjunctive therapies: an H2 -blocker (e.g. ranitidine, famotidine) 3 - add a leukotriene receptor antagonist (e.g. montelukast) , Page 11 of 13 4- Add a short-acting sedating H1 at bedtime (e.g. hydroxyzine) for sleep if symptoms interrupt rest Short-course corticosteroids: In severe acute urticaria or angioedema flares, a brief prednisone/prednisolone course (≈0.5–1 mg/kg daily, 3–10 days) Management of chronic urticaria • Trigger avoidance and first-line therapy • Second-line – Up-dose and add-ons • Third-line – Refractory therapy: 1- potent antihistamine or tricyclic with high H1-blocking effect (e.g. doxepin 10–50 mg) 2- omalizumab (anti-IgE) 300 mg subcutaneously every 4 weeks (in patients ≥12 years) • Fourth-line – Immunosuppressants: cyclosporine (3 –5 mg/kg/day, with blood pressure and renal monitoring) Management of physical urticarias • Trigger avoidance and prophylaxis. For example, cold urticaria: avoid cold exposure; cholinergic urticaria: avoid overheating; dermographism: avoid scratching; exercise-induced: take an H1- antihistamine before exertion. • Manage with the same antihistamine-based algorithm as CSU. Management of urticaria vasculitis 1-Laboratory investigations for associated diseases: • CBC with differential, platelet count; ESR, CRP; LFTs, BUN, and Crt • Complement assays – C3, C4, CH50; if C4 low, C1q • Urinalysis • ANA, anti-Ro Ab 2- Antihistamines for associated pruritus 3- NSAIDs – improvement in 50% of pts 4- Colchicine, dapsone, hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, plasmapheresis 5- Corticosteroids ± immunosuppressants Angioedema without urticaria • Affect any part of the body, but the commonest sites are the lips, eyelids and genitalia. • The tongue and pharynx may also be affected. • Individual lesions may be single or multiple and may appear with dramatic suddenness. Page 12 of 13 • Itching is often absent. • The lesions last for a few hours, or occasionally persist for 2–3 days Angioedema Page 13 of 13 Management Angioedema Histaminergic Angioedema (often allergic, with urticaria) Typical causes: Food, insect stings, drugs (e.g., penicillin), etc. Treatment: 1. Epinephrine IM (0.3–0.5 mg) — if anaphylaxis or airway threat 2. H1-antihistamines: e.g., diphenhydramine, cetirizine 3. H2-antihistamines: e.g., ranitidine, famotidine 4. Systemic corticosteroids: e.g., prednisone or methylprednisolone 5. Supportive care: IV fluids, oxygen if needed Non-Histaminergic Angioedema Usually bradykinin-mediated, such as: a. ACE inhibitor-induced angioedema, Stop ACE inhibitor immediately • Antihistamines & corticosteroids may not be effective • Supportive care ± ICU admission if airway is threatened • Icatibant (bradykinin receptor antagonist) — may help in severe cases B- Hereditary Angioedema (HAE) Caused by C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency Treatment during attacks: 1. C1 esterase inhibitor concentrate (Berinert, Cinryze) 2. Icatibant 3. Ecallantide (kallikrein inhibitor) 4. Prophylaxis (if frequent/severe attacks): androgens (danazol), lanadelumab, or prophylactic C1-INH

name: Parasitic infestations
text: Page 1 of 7 No Parasitic Skin Infestations SLOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Describe clinical presentations and types of scabies 2. Describe the clinical presentation of lice infestations 3. Complete a clinical assessment, order the appropriate investigation(s) and prescribe the correct management of scabies and pediculosis. Scabies ➢ Scabies is a worldwide problem with all ages, races, and socioeconomic groups being susceptible. ➢ Environmental factors that promote its spread include overcrowding, institutional settings, delayed treatment, and lack of public awareness of the condition. Mode of transmission Scabies can be transmitted directly by close personal contact, sexual or otherwise, or indirectly via fomites. Causative organism The species-specific, eight-legged mite adult female Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis causes human scabies. The scabies mite is 0.35 × 0.3 mm in size and too small to be seen by the naked eye. (Figure 1) The entire 30-day life cycle of these mites is completed within the epidermis. Each day a female mite lays 2–3 eggs, which require approximately 10 days to mature. The number of mites living on an infested host can vary greatly, although there are usually fewer than a hundred and often no more than 10–15. However, patients with crusted scabies may have thousands of mites on their skin surface, and live mites can be recovered in debris from sheets, the floor, curtains, and chairs in the environment of affected individuals. Figure 1 – Female Sarcoptes Scabii Page 2 of 7 Clinical picture of classic scabies The incubation period before symptoms develop can range from days to months. In first-time infestations, it usually takes 2–6 weeks before the host’s immune system becomes sensitized to the mite or its by-products, resulting in pruritus and cutaneous lesions. In contrast, a subsequent infestation often becomes symptomatic within 24–48 hours. The epidemiologic history (nocturnal pruritus, pruritus of a scratching nature, pruritus in household members or other close personal contacts), the distribution and types of lesions, form the basis of the clinical diagnosis. The intense pruritus is classically accentuated at night and by a hot bath or shower. Pruritus may be present before any overt physical signs appear. Cutaneous lesions are symmetrical, typically involving the interdigital web spaces of the hands, flexural aspect of the wrists, axillae, posterior auricular area, waist (including the umbilicus), ankles, feet, and buttocks. In men, penile and scrotal lesions are common, while in women, the areolae, nipples, and vulvar area are often affected. In infants, the elderly and immunocompromised hosts, all skin surfaces are susceptible, including the scalp and face. Lesions are polymorphic. Typically, small erythematous papules are present in association with a variable degree of excoriation and linear scratch marks are seen. Vesicles, indurated nodules, and eczematous dermatitis are also common. The pathognomonic sign is the burrow, representing the tunnel that a female mite excavates while laying eggs. Clinically, the burrow is wavy, thread-like, grayish-white, and 1–10 mm in length. Many patients, however, do not have obvious burrows on inspection, Secondary bacterial infections with Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes sometimes complicate scabies. Investigations Confirmation of the diagnosis can be achieved by light microscopic examination of mineral oil preparations of skin scrapings (from infested areas) for adult mites, eggs, and/or fecal pellets (scybala). A scalpel or curette or transparent adhesive tapes may be used to obtain the skin sample. Dermoscopy and confocal microscopy can prove useful for direct in vivo visualization of mites and eggs. A skin biopsy may confirm the clinical diagnosis, but only if the specimen obtained happens to contain the mite or its eggs. Often, however, the diagnosis is a clinical one, resting on history and physical findings (e.g. burrows, genital lesions) as well as response to treatment. Clinical types Animal scabies Zoonotic scabies and scab mites may affect humans who come in close contact with the animal. The reaction resembles scabies but typically runs a self-limited course. Burrows are usually absent. Page 3 of 7 Infantile scabies Acral vesiculopustules can represent a clue to the diagnosis of scabies in infants. Crusted/ Norwegean scabies The crusted variant, Norwegian scabies, can have up into millions of mites on a single individual. Crusted scabies occurs in patients who are immunocompromised due to immunosuppressive therapy, diabetes, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), or older age. This high density requires only short contact with patients and contaminated materials for infection to occur.Crusted scabies often manifests with marke hyperkeratosis that favors acral sites including subungual areas but involvement may be widespread. Nodular scabies The nodular form of scabies is a variant of the classic form. This form presents with erythematous nodules with a predilection towards the axilla and groin. The nodules are pruritic and considered to be a hypersensitivity reaction to the female mite. Treatment Close contacts should be treated. Machine wash and dry all bedding/clothes items using hot water and high heat cycles (temperatures in excess of 50 degrees C for 10 minutes will kill mites and eggs). 1- Scabies treatment includes administration of a scabicidal agent, as well as an appropriate antimicrobial agent if a secondary infection has developed. The mainstay of scabies treatment is the application of topical scabicidal agents, with repeat application in 7 days. • The treatment of choice is permethrin 5% lotion, which has been approved by the FDA for treatment of scabies in patients aged 2 months or older and has been listed as first- line therapy by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). • Crotamiton lotion 10% - This agent is FDA-approved for treatment of scabies in adults but not in children; treatment failure is frequent. • Sulfur ointment 5-10% - it is safe for topical use in children, including those younger than 2 months • Malathion lotion 0.5% • Spinosad topical suspension 0.9%. This agent is FDA-approved for treatment of scabies in patients aged 4 years or older. • Lindane lotion 1% . • Benzyl benzoate, an ester of benzoic acid and benzyl alcohol, is neurotoxic to mites and has been used to treat scabies. 2- Antipruritic therapy • Itching may persist for up to a month, even following successful treatment. Pruritus may be partially alleviated with an oral antihistamine. • Intranodular injection of dilute corticosteroids may be necessary in cases of nodular scabies Page 4 of 7 3- Systemic treatment Ivermectin also is believed to act as an agonist of the neurotransmitter gamma- aminobutyric acid (GABA), thereby disrupting GABA-mediated central nervous system (CNS) neurosynaptic transmission, resulting in paralysis and death of the parasite. Ivermectin is used for crusted scabies, in large-scale outbreaks as in crowded settings like nursing homes, hospitals, or institutional facilities, and in patients with impaired immunity such as those with HIV, are at higher risk for severe infestations like crusted scabies. Two 200-µg/kg doses should be taken orally with food 7-14 days apart. It is contraindicated in pregnancy, lactation and children under 5 years of age. 4- Treatment of secondary infection Management of crusted scabies • Initiate contact precautions and isolate the affected individual from other patients • Initiate medical treatment: ➢ Head to toe permethrin cream daily × 7 days AND ➢ Ivermectin 0.2 mg/kg/dose (14 mg for 70 kg individual) on days 1, 2, 8, 9, and 15 • Trim nails and use a nail brush to remove mites •Machine wash and dry all bedding/clothes items using hot water and high heat cycles (temperatures in excess of 50 degrees C for 10 minutes will kill mites and eggs) • Includes bedding/cloth

name: Syphilis & gonorrhea
text: 8 Syphilis, leukorrhea and urethral discharge SLOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Describe the clinical features of primary, secondary and tertiary syphilis 2. Describe clinical features of gonococcal urethritis and DD 3. Describe the diagnostic work-up, particularly serologic tests of syphilis and gonorrhea 4. Explain the main treatments Syphilis Syphilis, also known as lues, is a contagious, sexually transmitted disease caused by the spirochete Treponema pallidum subspecies pallidum. The only known host is the human. The spirochete enters through the skin or mucous membranes, where the primary manifestations are seen. In congenital syphilis, the treponeme crosses the placenta and infects the fetus. The risk of acquiring infection from sexual contact with an infected partner in the previous 30 days is 16–30%. Syphilis results in multiple patterns of skin and visceral disease that can be lifelong. Treponema pallidum T. pallidum is a delicate, spiral spirochete that is actively motile. The number of spirals varies from 4 to 14, and the entire length is 5–20 µm. The motility is characteristic, consisting of three movements: a projection in the direction of the long axis, a rotation on its long axis, and a bending in the middle. The precise uniformity of the spiral coils is not distorted during these movements. It can be demonstrated in preparations from fresh primary or secondary lesions by darkfield microscopy or by fluorescent antibody techniques. Microscopic characteristics of T. pallidum cannot be distinguished from commensal oral treponemes, so darkfield examination of oral lesions is unreliable. Direct fluorescent antibody testing can be used for confirmation. T. pallidum is an effective pathogen because it disseminates widely and rapidly after infection. It is in the bloodstream within hours of intratesticular injection and in numerous organs, including the brain, within 18 hours after inoculation. Figure 1: Positive dark field microscopy for T. pallidum (Dermatology, 5th Edition By Jean L. Bolognia, 2024) Serologic testing Serologic testing are either “treponemal” or “nontreponemal.” Treponemal tests detect specific antitreponemal antibodies by enzyme immunoassay (EIA) or T. pallidum particle assay (TPPA). These new treponemal tests have specificity and sensitivity exceeding 95%, even in patients with primary syphilis. Nontreponemal tests are based on the fact that serum of persons with syphilis aggregates a cardiolipin-cholesterol-lecithin antigen. This aggregation can be viewed directly in tubes or on cards or slides, or it can be examined in an autoanalyzer. Because these tests use lipoidal antigens rather than T. pallidum or its components, they are called nontreponemal antigen tests. The most widely used nontreponemal tests are the rapid plasma reagin (RPR) and VDRL tests. These nontreponemal tests become positive within 5–6 weeks of infection, shortly before the chancre heals. The treponemal tests include the microhemagglutination assay for T. pallidum (MHA- TP) , the fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption (FTA-ABS) test, enzyme immunoassay (EIA), and T. pallidum particle assay (TPPA). EIA tests are available that detect both IgG- and IgM-specific antibodies against T. pallidum. The IgM becomes detectable 2–3 weeks after infection, about the time the chancre appears. The IgG test becomes positive at 4–5 weeks; thus the IgM test is much more useful in diagnosing primary syphilis. These specific treponemal tests are also positive earlier than the nontreponemal tests and may be used to confirm the diagnosis of primary syphilis in a patient with a negative RPR/ VDRL. The EIA, TPPA, FTA-ABS, and MHA-TP remain positive for life in the majority of patients, although these tests will become negative with treatment in 13–24% of patients, regardless of stage and HIV status. The IgM EIA test, however, becomes negative after treatment in early syphilis, so that at 1 year 92% of these patients are negative on the IgM EIA. Primary Stage (Chancre) The chancre is usually the first cutaneous lesion, appearing 18–21 days after infection. The typical chancre is a small red papule or a crusted superficial erosion. In a few days to weeks, it becomes a round or oval, indurated, slightly elevated papule, with an eroded but not ulcerated surface that exudes a serous fluid . On palpation, it has a cartilage-like consistency. The lesion is usually painless. The regional lymph nodes on one or both sides are usually enlarged, firm, and nontender and do not suppurate. Adenopathy begins 1 or 2 weeks after the chancre appears. The classical chancre leaves no scar when it heals. Chancres generally occur singly Figure 2: Syphilitic chancre (Dermatology, 5th Edition By Jean L. Bolognia, 2024) Secondary Syphilis The skin manifestations of secondary syphilis occur in 80% or more of patients with secondary syphilis. The early eruptions are symmetric, more or less generalized, superficial, nondestructive, exanthematous, transient, and macular; later they are maculopapular or papular eruptions, which are usually polymorphous scaly. The early manifestations tend to be distributed over the face, shoulders, flanks, palms and soles, and anal or genital regions. The presence of lesions on the palms and soles is strongly suggestive of syphilis. The earliest form of macular secondary syphilis begins with the appearance of an exanthematous erythema 6–8 weeks after the development of the chancre, which may still be present. Simultaneous with the onset of the eruption, there is a generalized shotty adenopathy, most readily palpable in the posterior cervical, axillary, and epitrochlear areas. Papular eruptions usually arise slightly later than the macular eruption. The fully developed lesions are round and of a coppery shade ( Psoriasiform eruption may occur. Split papules are hypertrophic, fissured papules that form in the creases of the alae nasi and at the oral commissures. These may persist for a long period. Condylomata lata are indurated lesions, relatively broad and flat, located mainly around the genitalia and anus. They may become hypertrophic and, protrude above the surface, forming a soft, red, often mushroom-like mass 1–3 cm in diameter, usually with a smooth, moist, weeping, gray surface. Condyloma lata may be lobulated but are not covered by the digitate elevations characteristic of venereal warts (condylomata acuminata). Syphilitic alopecia is irregularly distributed so that the scalp has a moth-eaten appearance. Mucous membrane lesions are present in one-third of patients with secondary syphilis and may be the only manifestation of the infection. The most common mucosal lesion in the early phase is the syphilitic sore throat, a diffuse pharyngitis that may be associated with tonsillitis or laryngitis. Hoarseness and sometimes complete aphonia may be present. On the tongue, smooth, small or large, well-defined patches devoid of papillae may be seen, most frequently on the dorsum near the median raphe. Ulcerations may occur on the tongue and lips during the late secondary period, at times resembling aphthae or major aphthae. Mucous patches are the most characteristic mucous membrane lesions of secondary syphilis. They are macerated, flat, grayish, rounded erosions covered by a delicate, soggy membrane. These highly infectious lesions are about 5 mm in diameter and are full of treponemes. They occur on the tonsils, tongue, pharynx, gums, lips, and buccal areas or on the genitalia, chiefly in women, in whom the lesions are most common on the labia minora, vaginal mucosa, and cervix. text: Page 1 of 12 No Acne SLOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Describe the epidemiology, pathophysiology and common presentations of acne and acneiform eruptions. 2. Describe treatment algorithm for comedonal, papulopustular, nodular acne. 3. Recognize optimal use and adverse events of topical and systemic drugs for acne. 4. Develop the ability to make differential diagnoses, by comparing and contrasting the features of acne vulgaris, rosacea, hidradenitis suppurativa. Acne vulgaris Sebaceous glands are almost always associated with hair follicles except for the free sebaceous glands found on the vermilion lips and oral mucosa (Fordyce spots or granules), eyelids (meibomian glands), areolae (Montgomery tubercles), and labia minora and prepuce (Tyson glands). Sebaceous glands produce sebum, which is released into the infundibular portion of the hair follicle. Sebum production increases at the time of puberty and is a critical factor in the pathogenesis of acne vulgaris. Prevalence of acne vulgaris With a peak incidence during adolescence, acne affects ~85% of young people between 12 and 24 years of age. Nevertheless, preadolescent acne affects children 7 to 11 years of age and acne may continue into adulthood. Pathogenesis The principal abnormality in acne is comedo formation. It is produced by the impaction and distention of the follicles with a keratinous plug in the lower infundibulum. The keratinous plug is caused by hyperproliferation and abnormal differentiation of keratinocytes. Androgens, alterations in lipid composition, and an abnormal response to local cytokines are all hypothesized to be important. Androgen stimulation of the sebaceous glands is critical. As the retained cells block the follicular opening, the lower portion of the follicle is dilated by entrapped sebum. Disruption of the follicular epithelium permits discharge of the follicular contents into the dermis. The combination of keratin, sebum, and microorganisms, particularly Cutibacterium acnes, leads to the release of proinflammatory mediators and the accumulation of lymphocytes, neutrophils, and foreign body giant cells. This in turn causes the formation of inflammatory papules, pustules, and nodulocystic lesions. (Figure 1) Page 2 of 12 Figure 1: Pathogenesis of acne The development of acne involves the complex interplay of four main factors: (1) follicular hyperkeratinization; (2) hormonal influences on sebum production and composition; (3) inflammation; (4) C. acnes residing in the sebaceous follicle Follicular Hyperkeratinization The microcomedo is thought to be the precursor of all clinically apparent acne lesions. Corneocytes, which are normally shed into the hair follicle lumen and extruded, accumulate due to increases in both follicular keratinocyte proliferation and corneocyte cohesiveness, leading to the development of a hyperkeratotic plug that acts as a bottle neck. Hormonal Influences on Sebum Production and Composition Sebum production is controlled primarily by androgens, with additional influences from other hormones and neuropeptides. Androgens are produced both outside the pilosebaceous unit, mainly by the gonads and adrenal glands, and locally within the sebaceous gland via the action of androgen-metabolizing enzymes such as 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (HSD), 17β-HSD and 5α-reductase. Androgen receptors, found in the cells of the basal layer of the sebaceous gland and the outer root sheath of the hair follicle, are responsive to testosterone and 5α-dihydrotestosterone (DHT), the most potent androgens. Inflammation in acne: It is clear that when a follicle involved with acne ruptures, it exudes keratin, sebum, C. acnes, and cellular debris into the surrounding dermis, thereby intensifying inflammation. Nevertheless, inflammation is also seen early in acne lesion formation. Page 3 of 12 Cutibacterium acnes colonization and activities C. acnes is a Gram-positive, anaerobic/microaerophilic rod that is found on the skin surface and within the sebaceous follicle. Through activation of the TLR2 pathway, C. acnes stimulates the release of proinflammatory mediators such as IL-1α, IL-8, IL-12, tumor necrosis factor (TNF), and matrix metalloproteinases. IL-8 leads to neutrophil recruitment, the release of lysosomal enzymes, and subsequent disruption of the follicular epithelium, while IL-12 promotes Th1 responses. Dietary Factors The relationship between diet and acne remains controversial. Several observational studies have found that the intake of milk, especially skim milk, is positively associated with acne prevalence and severity. Exacerbation of acne with the use of whey protein supplements for body building has also been reported. Vitamin B12 supplementation can potentially trigger the development of acne or an acneiform eruption by altering the transcriptome of skin microbiota, leading to increased production of proinflammatory porphyrins by Cutibacterium acnes. Clinical picture Acne is typically found in sites with well-developed sebaceous glands, most often the face and upper trunk. Despite evidence that inflammation is present in even the earliest comedones , acne lesions are divided into non-inflammatory and inflammatory groups based upon their clinical appearance. (Figures 2 &3) Non-inflammatory acne is characterized by open and closed comedones. Closed comedones (whiteheads) are generally small (~1 mm), skin -colored papules with no apparent follicular opening or associated erythema. Open comedones (blackheads) have a conspicuous dilated follicular opening that is filled with an inspissated core of shed keratin. Melanin deposition and lipid oxidation within the debris may be responsible for the black color. Inflammatory acne is characterized by papules, pustules, and nodules of varying severity. Erythematous papules typically range from 1 to 5 mm in diameter. Pustules tend to be approximately equal in size and are filled with white purulent material and normal microbiota, including C. acnes. As the severity of lesions progresses, nodules form and become markedly inflamed, indurated, and tender. The pseudocysts of acne are deeper and filled with a combination of pus and serosanguineous fluid. Figure 2: Types of acne lesions Page 4 of 12 Figure 3: Comedones, nodules, acne scars Acne variants: Acne fulminans Acne fulminans is the most severe form of acne and is characterized by the abrupt development of nodular and suppurative acne lesions in association with systemic manifestations. This uncommon variant primarily affects boys 13 –16 years of age. Osteolytic bone lesions may accompany the cutaneous findings. Systemic manifestations include fever, arthralgias, myalgias, hepatosplenomegaly, and severe malaise. Erythema nodosum may also arise in association with acne fulminans. Laboratory abnormalities include an elevated ESR, proteinuria, leukocytosis, and anemia, Recommended treatment of acne fulminans includes prednisone 0.5– 1 mg/kg/day as monotherapy for at least 2 –4 weeks, followed by initiation of low-dose isotretinoin (e.g. 0.1 mg/kg/day) after the acute inflammation subsides; after at least 4 weeks of this combination, the isotretinoin dose can be slowly increased and the prednisone tapered over a period of 1 –2 months . (Figure 4) Figure 4: Acne fulminans Acne excoriée Acne excoriée occurs more often in young women. Typical comedones and inflammatory papules are systematically excoriated in a ritualistic manner, leaving crusted erosions that may scar. Linear erosions suggest self-manipulation, and an underlying psychiatric component should be considered. Individuals with an anxiety, obsessive– compulsive, or body dysmorphic disorder are particularly at risk, and antidepressants or psychotherapy may be helpful in these patients. text: Page 1 of 9 No LASERS in Dermatology SLOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Describe principles, indications of vascular lasers 2. Describe principles, indications of pigment lasers 3. Describe principles, indications of hair reduction lasers 4. Describe principles, indications of ablative lasers Lasers Cutaneous laser surgery is a continually evolving area of dermatology. Development of new lasers, as well as improvements in existing lasers, continues to advance the field. “Laser” is an acronym for Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation. ➢ Compared with other light sources, laser light is defined as monochromatic (i.e., a single wavelength), collimated (i.e., nondivergent), and coherent (i.e., in phase, with peaks and troughs of the light all aligned). (Figure 1) Figure 1 – Characteristics of LASER. ➢ Laser tissue interaction Light can interact with incident targets in one of several ways: reflected, transmitted, scattered, or absorbed. When reflected, transmitted, or scattered, the light has no effect on the target tissue. When absorbed, however, the light energy is transformed into heat. In most cases of laser therapy, it is the heat generated by absorption that produces the desired therapeutic effect. The concept of selective photothermolysis, originally promoted is the basis for all laser-tissue interactions. A particular target chromophore absorbs light and is selectively damaged or destroyed. The endogenous chromophores of importance are melanin, haemoglobin, water and collagen. Page 2 of 9 Lasers are usually named after the constituents of the active or gain medium, which may be a gas, liquid, solid or semiconductor. The active medium is contained within an optical cavity. In its simplest form the optical cavity consists of two opposing mirrors, one of which is fully reflective and the other, the output coupler, is partly transparent. Photons moving parallel to the axis of the optical cavity are reflected between the two mirrors, in turn eliciting stimulated emission in the same axis. The energy required for the process of light amplification is supplied by an external source such as an electric current (if the active medium is a gas) or by a light source (flash lamp or other laser. This supply of energy is called optical pumping and amplifies the light until it is emitted through the output coupler. It then enters a delivery system that transmits it to the operator hand-piece. (Figure 2) Figure 2 – Laser system Applications of laser principles Vascular lesions and vascular lasers Target chromophore: Oxyhaemoglobin. Oxyhemoglobin has an absorption band at 577 nm. Examples of indications: port-wine birthmarks, telangiectasias, erythematous scars, and hemangiomas. (Figures 3-6) Figure 3 – Erythematous scars Page 3 of 9 Figure 4 - Telengiectasia Figure 5 – Portwine stain Figure 6 - Haemangioma Page 4 of 9 Examples of vascular lasers (Figure 7) Figure 7 – Vascular lasers Tattoo and pigment lasers Light tissue interaction: Melanosomes are melanin-containing organelles that range from ~0.3–1 micron in size, and they can act as a primary target for selective photothermolysis of pigmented lesions. Melanin has a broad absorption spectrum, which lends itself to possible targeting by a wide range of lasers. When the fluence threshold for melanosome disruption is reached, the melanin-containing cell dies, and Q-switched lasers are able to selectively target individual pigmented cells. Treatment of tattoos with Q-switched nanosecond or picosecond lasers fragments the ink particles and selectively kills pigment containing cells, with resultant ink particle release. Subsequent removal of tattoo ink particles can occur via an epidermal crust and/or lymphatic transport while some particles are rephagocytosed by dermal cells. Examples of indications: tattoos, epidermal lesions as freckles, café au lait macules and dermal melanocytosis as nevi of ota, drug induced pigmentation. (Figure 8) Figure 8 – Nevus of Otta, freckles, café au lait macule (some indication for pigment lasers) Page 5 of 9 Examples of devices for treating tattoos and pigmented lesions: Q-switched Nd:YAG (1064 nm) laser and Q-switched frequency doubled Nd:YAG (532 nm) laser: for the removal of epidermal pigment. Q-switched ruby (694 nm), alexandrite (755 nm) and diode (810 nm) lasers: for deeper dermal penetration. Hair reduction lasers Light is probably absorbed by melanin in the hair shaft and matrix but it is likely that heat is then transferred to the true target structures, stem cells (mainly in the bulge area of the outer root sheath) and possibly blood vessels in the papilla. ➢ Devices for hair reduction: The normal mode ruby (694 nm), alexandrite (755 nm), diode (800 nm) and Nd:YAG (1064 nm) lasers have all been used for photoepilation. Some indications for hair reduction (Figure 9) ➢ Hirsutism ➢ Hypertrichosis ➢ Hairy congenital nevi ➢ Hair bearing skin grafts ➢ Pseudofolliculitis Figure 9 – Hirsutism, pseuodofolliculitis barbae. The CO2 laser (10 600 nm) can be used as an incisional or resurfacing instrument. Tissue can be incised by using a high-power, focused beam that vaporizes the tissue in its immediate path. 2. Ablative laser resurfacing. This was performed initially with scanned CO2 lasers, the immediate effect of which is ablation (or vaporization) of the epidermis and sometimes the superficial papillary dermis. Carbon dioxide (10 600 nm) laser and Er: YAG lasers The CO2 laser produces light (10 600 nm) that is relatively poorly absorbed by the chromophore water, and which therefore penetrates relatively deeply (30 μm). Examples of indications: Epidermal nevi, epidermal neoplasms, actinic keratosis, benign cutaneous proliferations (eg seborrheic keratosis, viral warts, syringomas), dermal infiltrates (eg xanthelasma), acne scars, skin aging. text: Page 1 of 8 No Bullous Dermatoses SLOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Describe the pathogenesis (pemphigus, bullous pemphigoid, dermatitis herpetiformis) 2. Differentiate and describe lesions starting from clinical cases. 3. Describe the histopathology, enumerate investigations. 4. Explain the main treatments including biologics. 1. Pemphigus ➢ Pemphigus is a group of autoimmune blistering diseases of the skin and mucous membranes that is characterized by: histologically, intraepidermal blisters due to the loss of cell–cell adhesion of keratinocytes, immunopathologically the finding of in vivo bound and circulating IgG autoantibodies directed against the cell surface of keratinocytes. Clinical types Two main types; Pemphigus vulgaris and pemphigus foliaceus. Pemphigus vegetans is a variant of pemphigus vulgaris, and pemphigus erythematosus and fogo selvagem represent localized and endemic variants of pemphigus foliaceus, respectively. Pathogenesis Autoantibodies are directed against the cell surface of keratinocytes, resulting in the loss of cell–cell adhesion of keratinocytes through a process called acantholysis. The functional inhibition of desmogleins, which play an important role in cell–cell adhesion of keratinocytes, by IgG autoantibodies results in blister formation. Patients with pemphigus vulgaris and pemphigus foliaceus have IgG autoantibodies against desmoglein 3 and desmoglein 1, respectively. (Figure 1) Figure 1– Pathogenesis of pemphigus Page 2 of 8 Clinical picture The mean age of onset of disease is 50 to 60 years, although the range is broad and disease arising in the elderly and in children has been described. Mucous membrane lesions usually present as painful erosions. Intact blisters are rare, in the oral cavity, the most common sites are the buccal and palatine mucosae. The erosions are painful, may result in decreased oral intake of food or liquids. Involvement of the throat produces hoarseness and difficulty in swallowing. The oesophagus also may be involved and sloughing of its entire lining in the form of a cast has been reported. The conjunctivae, nasal mucosa, vagina, labia, penis and anus can develop lesions as well. (Figure 2) The primary skin lesions of pemphigus vulgaris are flaccid, thin walled, easily ruptured blisters. They can appear anywhere on the skin surface and arise on either normal- appearing skin or erythematous bases. The blisters are fragile and soon rupture to form painful erosions that ooze and bleed easily. These erosions often attain a large size and can become generalized. The erosions soon become partially covered with crusts. (Figure 1) Because of an absence of cohesion within the epidermis, its upper layers easily move laterally with slight pressure or rubbing in patients with active disease (Nikolsky sign). The lack of cohesion of the skin may also be demonstrated with the “bulla-spread phenomenon” – gentle pressure on an intact bulla forces the fluid to spread under the skin away from the site of pressure (Asboe–Hansen sign). Figure 2 – Mucous membrane erosions, flaccid cutaneous bullae in pemphigus vulgaris. Pemphigus vegetans is a rare vegetative variant of pemphigus vulgaris. Pemphigus vegetans is characterized by flaccid blisters that become erosions and then form fungoid vegetations or papillomatous proliferations. Pemphigus Foliaceus Patients with pemphigus foliaceus develop scaly, crusted cutaneous erosions, often on an erythematous base, but they do not have clinically apparent mucosal involvement even with widespread disease. Page 3 of 8 Pemphigus erythematosus is simply a localized variant of pemphigus foliaceus. Typical scaly and crusted lesions of pemphigus foliaceus appear in “seborrheic” areas. Diagnosis Histopathologic examination In pemphigus vulgaris the characteristic histologic finding in this form of pemphigus is intraepidermal blister formation due to a loss of cell–cell adhesion of keratinocytes (acantholysis). Acantholysis occurs just above the basal cell layer (suprabasilar acantholysis). A few rounded-up (acantholytic) keratinocytes are often seen within the blister cavity. Although the basal cells lose lateral desmosomal contact with their neighbors, they maintain their attachment to the basement membrane via hemidesmosomes, thus giving the appearance of a “row of tombstones” the dermis there is a moderate perivascular mononuclear cell infiltrate.(Figure 3A) Figure 3 – A: Suprabasal acantholysis, with characteristic tombstone appearance of basal cell layer. B: Subcorneal intragranular acantholysis. In pemphigus vegetans, suprabasilar acantholysis is seen, in addition to considerable papillomatosis and acanthosis. In pemphigus foliaceus, there is acantholysis in the upper epidermis, within or adjacent to the granular layer (subcorneal intragranular). The dermis shows a moderate number of inflammatory cells. (Figure 2B) ELISA is increasingly being used to detect antigen-specific autoantibodies for the diagnosis of pemphigus. The patient’s serum is tested on ELISA plates pre-coated with relevant recombinant proteins, e.g. Dsg1, Dsg3. Thus, specific antibodies directed against desmogleins can be detected. Page 4 of 8 Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) examines patients’ skin or mucous membranes in order to demonstrate in vivo bound IgG deposition on the keratinocyte cell surfaces (honey-comb appearance). DIF is the most reliable and sensitive diagnostic test for all forms of pemphigus. (Figure 4) Figure 4 – Direct immunofluorescence in pemphigus showing honey comb appearance Indirect immunofluorescence (IIF) examines patients’ sera in order to demonstrate circulating IgG autoantibodies directed against epithelial cell surfaces. Treatment Before the advent of systemic corticosteroids, pemphigus vulgaris was usually a fatal disease; most patients died within 2–5 years of the onset of the disease because large areas of the skin lost their epidermal barrier function, leading to the loss of body fluids or to secondary bacterial infections. Systemic corticosteroid therapy, usually in the form of oral prednisone, is standard treatment. Prednisone at 1 mg/kg/day is a typical initial dosage. Other immune suppressants In general, immunosuppressive agents, such as azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil and cyclophosphamide, when combined with corticosteroids, may result in gaining early control of the disease and an increased percentage of clinical remissions. Plasmapheresis is useful for quickly reducing the titers of circulating autoantibodies and should be considered for severe pemphigus if the disease is unresponsive to a combination of prednisone and immunosuppressives. High-dose IVIg is another option for resistant disease. IVIg is a blood product prepared from pooled plasma that has immunomodulatory effects when used in a high dose. Page 5 of 8 Rituximab is a potent B cell-depleting chimeric anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody that was first used to treat B cell malignancies, but increasingly is used for a variety of autoimmune diseases, including pemphigus. Local skin care The skin lesions are extremely painful in advanced cases. When there are extensive raw surfaces, prolonged daily baths are helpful in removing the thickened crusts and reducing the foul odour. Silver sulfadiazine (Silvadene) 1%, widely used for local therapy of burns, is an effective topical antimicrobial agent, suitable for treatment of limited disease. Management of complications of the disease; sepsis, fluid and electrolyte imbalance, hypoproteinemia. Management of complications of therapy; diabetes, hypertension, osteoporosis. Bullous pemphigoid Bullous pemphigoid (BP) is the most common autoimmune subepidermal blistering disease. BP is an example of an immune -mediated disease that is associated with a humoral and cellular response directed against two well-characterized self-antigens: BPAG2 and BPAG1 (structural components of the hemidesmosome). Lupus erythematosus: • Lupus erythematosus (LE) is usually divided into two main types: discoid LE (DLE) and systemic LE (SLE), with a third group, subacute cutaneous LE (SCLE). • Another classification: LE into three groups ; cutaneous LE, intermediate LE and SLE . • DLE can be subdivided into a localized form in which lesions are confined to the face above the chin, the scalp and the ears, and a disseminated form in which lesions also occur elsewhere on the body. • Discoid lupus erythematosus: • DLE is a benign inflammatory disorder of the skin, most frequently involving the face and scalp, and characterized by well-defined red, scaly patches of variable size, which heal with atrophy, scar ring and pigmentary changes. • DLE is one of the forms of cutaneous disease seen within the spectrum of LE: others are SCLE and acute cutaneous lupus, the latter seen in patients with the systemic form of the disease. • The disease may also be more generalized, affecting areas away from the face and scalp. • The incidence of cutaneous lupus was 4/100 000, with 80% being DLE. • There is a peak age of onset in the fourth decade in females and slightly later in males, although it can occur at any age. • The disease affects twice as many females as males. • • Clinical features: • The circumscribed or discoid form is the most frequent type of disease, and occurs particularly on the cheeks, bridge of the nose, ears, side of the neck and scalp. • Cicatrical Alopecia occurs in the scalp lesions. • Lesions occur as well-defined erythematous patches, varying in size from a few millimetres to 10–15 cm. • There is adherent scale in many cases, and when this is removed its undersurface shows horny plugs that have occupied dilated pilosebaceous canals. name: Psoriasis
text: No Psoriasis 1. Describe the epidemiology, pathophysiology and common presentations of psoriasis. 2. Describe histopathology. 3. Recognize different clinical types. 4. Recognize treatment lines. Psoriasis • Is a chronic , inflammatory and proliferative disease of the skin. • With multiple organ affection. • The most characteristic lesions consist of red, scaly, sharply demarcated, indurated plaques, present particularly over the extensor surfaces and scalp. • The extent and severity varies enormously over time and between individuals. Morphological variants are common. • Both genetic and environmental influences have a critical role in the aetiology and pathogenesis. Epidemiology: • There are two peak ages of incidence, the first occurring between 16 and 22 years and the second between 57 and 62 years of age. • Psoriasis affects adult men and women equally. Aetiology: • Genetics: Based on population data, lifetime risks of psoriasis are 4%, 28% and 65% if neither, one or both parents are affected. • Environmental factors: upper respiratory streptococcal infections may precipitate guttate psoriasis. • Medications: Many drugs have been reported to be responsible for the onset and/or exacerbation of psoriasis. • Both cigarette smoking and alchohol misuse are associated with developing severe forms of psoriasis. • The most important drugs involved in exacerbating psoriasis are : 1. Lithium. 2. Antimalarials. 3. Interferon gamma. 4. Beta blockers. 5. ACE inhibitors. 6. NSAIDS. 7. Although psoriasis may respond to oral corticosteroids, both tachyphylaxis and rebound phenomena occur. Withdrawal of corticosteroids may lead to rebound of the disease and the development of unstable psoriasis. • Psychological stress: Moderate to severe psoriasis is associated with increased levels of depression, anxiety . • Photoexposure: Although sunlight is generally beneficial, in 5–20% of patients psoriasis may be provoked by sunlight . • Trauma: Psoriasis can occur in sites of cutaneous trauma and old scars, the so‐called • Koebner phenomenon: appearance of isomorphic lesions on apparently normal skin following trauma during the active stage of the disease. Pathogensis: • The pathological abnormalities in psoriasis include hyperproliferation of the epidermis, a marked dermal and epidermal inflammatory infiltrate, increased angiogenesis within the dermis and abnormal cutaneous neuronal/neurotransmitter organization. • Normal basal keratinocytes proliferate, differentiate and ascend through the layers of the epidermis in a process takes that approximately 30 days in healthy individuals. • In psoriasis, this process only 4–5 days in active plaques. • Activated T cells are key in the pathogenesis of psoriasis. • Injury to the skin leads to activation of AMPs that binds to toll like receptors causing activation of dendritic cells that produces TNF‐α, IL‐6 and IL‐23. • This results in activation of Th17 cells, which in turn activate keratinocytes to proliferate and produce multiple chemokines and antimicrobial peptides . • In psoriasis plaques there are increased levels of IL‐2, IL‐8, interferon‐γ, γ TNF‐α, IL‐15, IL‐17, IL‐ 22 and IL‐23 . Histopathology: Epidermal changes: • There is parakeratosis . • Focal orthokeratosis . • Accumulation of neutrophils in the stratum corneum (munro microabscesses). • Near absence of the granular layer ( agranulosis, hypogranulosis). • Spongiform pustules in the malpighian layer • Regular Hyperplasia of the malpigian layer with elongation of rete ridges ( test tube acanthosis). • Suprapapillary epidermal thinning. Dermal changes: • Dilated, tortuous papillary blood vessels almost touch the undersurface of the thinning suprapapillary epidermis • Prescence of a mixed mononuclear and neutrophil infiltrate, as well as extravasated erythrocytes in the dilated cappillaries. Figure 1: psoriasis histopathology. Figure 2: psoriasis histopathology ( munro’s microabcess ). Clinical picture: Plaque psoriasis: • Is the most common type of psoriasis, accounting for about 80–90% of all cases . • Typical lesions are red scaly plaques, which are remarkably well demarcated from unaffected skin, with sharply delineated edges plaques may be encircled by a clear peripheral zone, the halo or ring of Woronoff , dusky red in colour and covered with silvery white lamellar scales. • Usually bilateral symmetrical distribution, variable in size. • Over the scalp, trunk and extensor surfaces of the limbs. • The successive removal of scales usually reveals an underlying smooth, glossy red membrane with small bleeding points where the thin suprapapillary epidermis has been torn off (Auspitz’s sign). • Figure 3: classical plaque psoriasis. Figure 4 : classical plaque psoriasis. ( Woronoff ring ). Figure 5: Koebner’s phenomenon in plaque psoriasis. Figure 6 : Auspitz Sign Scalp psoriasis: • The whole scalp may be diffusely involved, or multiple discrete plaques of varying size may be seen . Very thick plaques can develop, especially at the occiput. Plaques tend to be restricted to hair‐bearing areas, extending a short distance beyond the hairline and around the ears. Seborrhoeic psoriasis (sebopsoriasis): • Plaques of thin sharply demarcated erythema with variable scale may occur in the typical distribution of seborrhoeic dermatitis, involving paranasal areas, external ears, medial eye brows, hairline, presternal and interscapular chest wall . Flexural psoriasis (inverse psoriasis): • Psoriasis involving the inguinal creases, axillae, submammary folds, gluteal cleft, umbilicus and other body folds. • Flexural involvement is often seen in individuals with plaque psoriasis elsewhere on the skin. Figure 7: psoriasis in the umbilicus. • Flexural plaques are thin, scaling is greatly reduced or absent. • The surface has a glazed hue and fissuring at the depth of the skin fold is common, especially in the gluteal cleft. • • Figure 8 : flexural psoriasis. • • • • Non‐pustular palmoplantar psoriasis : • Psoriasis may present as typical scaly patches on which a fine silvery scale can be evoked by scratching; as less well‐defined plaques. • A sharply defined edge at the wrist, forearm or palm and absence of vesiculation are helpful to distinguish from eczema. • Nail psoriasis : • The nails grow more quickly in patients with psoriasis . • Nail dystrophy may be seen in association with all types of psoriasis or occasionally as an isolated feature. • Estimates of its incidence vary considerably. • nail changes are present in about 40% of cases at any point in time. Figure 9 : flexural psoriasis. • Psoriasis may affect any part of the nail unit, including the nail matrix, nail bed and hyponychium. • Nail psoriasis is associated with more extensive psoriasis, longer disease duration, family history of psoriasis and the presence of psoriatic arthritis. • Nail matrix disease presents with pits, ridges and grooves of the nail plate. Pitting is the most frequent change seen in fingernails, individual pits being uniform in size at about 1mm diameter and sometimes arranged longitudinally. • Nail bed disease can be seen as subungual ‘oil drops’ which are highly specific for psoriasis. Nail bed disease also causes subungual hyperkeratosis, splinter haemorrhages and distal onycholysis. • • • Figure 10 : nail psoriasis. • • • Mucosal lesions: • Geographic tongue (benign migratory glossitis) and fissured tongue are both more frequent among patients with psoriasis than healthy controls . It frequently follows several weeks after phanyngitis caused by group A streptococci, serological evidence for which can be found in about 60% of individuals. Describe the pathogenesis of xeroderma pigmentosa, clinical features, management lines 3. Describe the pathogenesis of neurofibromatosis, clinical features, diagnosis, screening for complications Ichthyosis Ichthyosis is not one disease but a group of diseases in which the homeostatic mechanism of epidermal cell kinetics or differentiation is altered, resulting in the clinical appearance of scale. Ichthyosis vulgaris This is the commonest form of inherited ichthyosis Inheritance pattern: Autosomal dominant Clinical picture ➢ Delayed onset after 3months ➢ Fine polygonal scales attached at the centre, free at the periphery on the skin with variable degree of dryness. Scales are coarser on lower limb than trunk. ➢ Manifestations are exacerbated during winter with great improvement in summer. ➢ Extensor aspect of extremities are most prominent while major body folds (eg axillary fold) are spared. ➢ Associated atopic manifestations: accentuated skin markings and hyperkeratosis of the palms are common features, and keratosis pilaris is frequently associated. (Figure 1) ➢ Prognosis: Benign course improve by age. Figure 1 – Ichthyosis scales, Palmar hyperkeratosis X-linked Ichthyosis: ➢ Inheritance pattern: X-linked recessive (exclusively affects males). ➢ Onset is usually before age 3 months. Cesarean birth is typical, with failure in progression of labor because of a placental sulfatase deficiency. Page 2 of 13 ➢ Scales are dark, large, and prominent on the anterior neck, extensor surfaces of the extremities and the trunk. (Figure 2) ➢ The sides of the neck are invariably involved, giving the child an unwashed look. ➢ The elbow and knee flexures are relatively spared, as are the face and scalp ➢ Palms and soles are almost always spared. ➢ Absent keratosis pilaris ➢ No increased AD ➢ Extracutaneous features: Cornaeal opacaities, cryptorchidism ➢ Prognosis: Unlike ichthyosis vulgaris, X-linked ichthyosis does not improve with age, but gradually worsens in both extent and severity. Figure 2 – X-linked ichthyosis Lamellar ichthyosis: ➢ Inheritance pattern: autosomal recessive ➢ Lamellar ichthyosis is present at birth, or becomes apparent soon after, and almost always involves the entire cutaneous surface. ➢ Usually, a collodion-like membrane encases the baby at birth, then desquamates over the first 2–3 weeks of life. (Figure 3) ➢ The ensuing ichthyosis is characterized by large, greyish brown scales, which are strikingly quadrilateral, free at the edges, and adherent in the center. ➢ In severe cases, the scales may be so thick that they are like armour plate. ➢ Moderate hyperkeratosis of the palms and soles is frequently present. ➢ Ectropion is usually present and is a helpful diagnostic sign. ➢ Prognosis: The most severe type of ichthyosis ➢ Histopathology: Hyperkeratosis is the consistent feature in the three types of ichthyoses. Page 3 of 13 Figure 3 – Collodion baby. Ectropion and facial affection in lamellar ichthyosis. Management of ichthyoses: ➢ In the milder types of ichthyosis the main treatment is regular application of moisturisers or emollients. ➢ These moisturisers are most effective when applied on wet skin within a couple of minutes of having a shower or bath. ➢ Keratolytics creams (keratolytics, e.g. salicylic acid) are sometimes used but they can irritate the skin and can be helpful on the palms and soles. ➢ Severe types of ichthyosis, systemic retinoid (synthetic vitamin A) tablet treatment may be suggested. Inheritance pattern: Autosomal recessive Clinical picture The disease is characterised by extreme photosensitivity. Cutaneous features: Age of onset: Early infancy/ first 2ys. Patients have marked photosensitivity in addition to an early onset for all major types of skin cancer. From an early age, many patients easily develop sunburns with erythema, edema and vesicles following minimal sun exposure, lentigines/freckles, mottled pigmentation. Actinic keratoses, basal cell carcinomas (BCCs), squamous cell carcinomas (SCCs), and less frequently, melanomas then develop in sun-exposed sites, also prematurely. (Figure 4) Skin cancer develops before age of 10ys BCC- SCC- less frequent MM. Most tumours occur on the head and neck. Ophthalmologic features Ocular abnormalities are almost as common as the cutaneous abnormalities, but they are strikingly limited to the anterior, UV -exposed structures of the eye (lids, cornea, and conjunctiva). Severe photophobia, keratitis, corneal opacification, and vascularization are common manifestations, while loss of eyelashes, ectropion, and SCC and melanoma of the UVR- exposed parts of the eyes are also frequently reported. Improves in summer Associated features AD KP Palmoplantar hyperkeratosis Palmoplantar hyperkeratosis Prognosis Improves with age Changes very little with age Treatment Emollient keratolytics Emollient keratolytics Emollient keratolytics Systemic retinoid (acitretin) Page 5 of 13 Systemic involvement There is an approximately 50-fold increase in internal neoplasms, especially of the central nervous system. Neurological; progressive neural degeneration in 20% of cases. Figure 4 – Ophthalmic and cutaneous manifestations in Xeroderma pigmentosum. Treatment As the skin changes are all caused by UV light, complete protection from exposure to UV can prevent further skin changes completely. Protective measures include the following: All windows should be covered with UV-resistant film When outside during daylight hours, exposed skin should be covered with sunscreen. Long trousers, long sleeves and gloves should be worn together with a UV -resistant face mask Systemic retinoids can prevent appearance of new cancers yet should be used for life so risk of side effects and rebound when stopped (cancer chemoprophylaxis). Epidermolysis Bullosa Epidermolysis bullosa (EB) is a group of rare genetic disorders that have in common the formation of blisters in response to minor physical injury. The EB conditions result from genetic defects of hemidesmosomes concerned with adhesion. Loss of adhesion results in blister formation. (Figure 5 & 6) Page 6 of 13 Clinical picture Blisters occur anywhere on the body but most commonly appear at sites of friction and minor trauma such as the feet and hands. text: Page 1 of 9 No Eczema SLOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Describe the epidemiology, pathophysiology, clinical presentation, diagnostic criteria of atopic dermatitis and main management lines 2. Recognize common presentations of eczematous eruptions (ear, eyelid, breast, hand, circumstomal, napkin, xerotic, elderly, hormonal) 1. What is Eczema?  Definition: Eczema, from the Greek ekzein ("to boil forth"), is a pattern of inflammatory skin reaction, not a single disease.  Clinical Features: 1. Acute: Red, swollen (edematous) plaques, sometimes with tiny grouped vesicles (blisters). 2. Subacute: Red plaques with scale or crusting. 3. Chronic: Dry scale or lichenification (thickened skin with prominent skin lines from chronic rubbing).  Key Symptom: Severe pruritus (itching) is a prominent feature, often worse at night and exacerbated by heat, sweat, and stress.  Histology: The hallmark of all eczematous reactions is spongiosis—serous fluid between epidermal cells—with a perivascular infiltrate of lymphocytes. Atopic Dermatitis (AD) - The "Itch that Rashes"  Definition: A chronic, inflammatory, and intensely pruritic skin disease with a course of exacerbations and remissions.  It's often the first step in the "atopic march," preceding food allergies, asthma, and allergic rhinitis.  Itching often begins before the rash appears Epidemiology of AD  Prevalence: A major global health issue, with prevalence dramatically increasing in the latter half of the 20th century.  Rates are up to 30% in developed nations and exceed 10% in many other countries.  Worldwide cumulative prevalence is around 20%.  Risk Factors:  Geography: High latitude and lower mean annual temperature. Page 2 of 9  Genetics: A strong genetic link exists. If both parents are atopic, the risk for a child developing allergic symptoms is ~79%.  Birth/Early Life: Cesarean delivery, first-born status, antibiotic exposure prenatally, and a "Western diet" alter the gut microbiome and increase risk. Pathophysiology of AD - A "Barrier-First" Disease  AD is a vicious cycle of a defective skin barrier and immune dysregulation.  Barrier Defect:  Genetic: Null mutations in the Filaggrin gene (FLG) are a major factor. Filaggrin is essential for creating the "natural moisturizing factor" (NMF) that keeps skin hydrated.  Reduced NMF leads to xerosis (dry skin) and increased transepidermal water loss (TEWL).  A compromised barrier allows allergens and microbes to penetrate the skin more easily.  Immune Dysregulation:  The barrier breach triggers a T-helper 2 (Th2) dominant immune response.  Keratinocytes release cytokines, which promotes Th2 inflammation.  Th2 cells release key cytokines:  IL-4 and IL-13: Drive the inflammatory feedback loop and further impair the barrier.  IL-31: Binds directly to nerves, causing intense itch, and also downregulates filaggrin expression. Clinical Presentation of AD - Age-Specific Patterns  Infantile AD (2 months - 2 years):  Begins as red, scaly patches, often on the cheeks.  Can spread to the scalp, forehead, and extensor surfaces of arms and legs.  Lesions are often exudative ("weepy") and crusted.  Childhood AD (2 - 10 years):  Classic "flexural" distribution: antecubital (elbow creases) and popliteal (knee creases) fossae. Page 3 of 9  Also affects the face, neck, wrists, and ankles.  Lesions are typically less weepy and more lichenified (thickened) from chronic scratching.  Adolescent/Adult AD:  Often involves flexural areas, neck, forehead, and around the eyes.  Lichenification and prurigo-like (intensely itchy, firm) papules are common.  Can present as localized eczema, especially on the hands, eyelids, or nipples. Infantile AD Childhood AD Page 4 of 9 Adult AD Diagnostic Criteria for AD (Hanifin & Rajka)  Diagnosis is clinical . No lab test is diagnostic. Criteria are used mainly for research but are helpful clinically.  Must have 3 of 4 MAJOR criteria:  Pruritus (itching).  Typical morphology and distribution (flexural for adults, facial/extensor for infants).  Chronic or chronically relapsing dermatitis.  Personal or family history of atopy (asthma, allergic rhinitis, AD).  Must ALSO have 3 or more MINOR criteria:  Xerosis (dry skin).  Ichthyosis / Hyperlinear palms / Keratosis pilaris.  Elevated serum IgE.  Early age of onset.  Tendency for skin infections (e.g., Staphylococcus aureus).  Nipple eczema.  Dennie-Morgan infraorbital fold (fold under the lower eyelid). Main Management Lines: The Stepped-Care Approach  Management is multifaceted, focusing on barrier repair, inflammation control, and trigger avoidance.  Foundation of Care: Barrier Repair & Education:  Moisturize! This is the cornerstone of AD care. Use thick, bland emollients (e.g., petrolatum-based) daily, especially after bathing ("soak and smear").  Gentle Cleansing: Use lukewarm water, limit soap, and choose non-soap, pH-balanced cleansers.  Education: A written action plan is crucial for patient/parent understanding and adherence.  Controlling Inflammation: Anti-inflammatory Topicals:  Topical Corticosteroids : First -line for flares. Potency is matched to body site and severity. Ointments are preferred. Page 5 of 9  Topical Calcineurin Inhibitors (TCIs) : Tacrolimus, Pimecrolimus. Excellent for sensitive areas (face, eyelids) and for maintenance therapy to prevent flares.  Topical PDE4 Inhibitors : Crisaborole. A non -steroidal option for mild -to-moderate AD.  Managing Itch & Infection:  Antipruritics: Sedating antihistamines (e.g., hydroxyzine) can help with sleep.  Antimicrobials:  Secondary bacterial infection (S. aureus) is common and causes flares.  Dilute bleach baths (e.g., ¼ cup in a full bathtub) twice weekly can reduce bacterial colonization and inflammation.  Topical or oral antibiotics may be needed for active infection.  Advanced Therapies for Severe/Refractory AD:  Phototherapy: Narrow-band UVB (NB-UVB) is highly effective.  Systemic Therapies:  Biologics: Dupilumab (injectable IL -4/IL-13 receptor inhibitor) is a targeted therapy that significantly reduces itch and rash.  Immunosuppressants: Cyclosporine, methotrexate, azathioprine, and others may be used for severe cases.  Systemic corticosteroids should be avoided for long -term use due to side effects and rebound flares Common Eczematous Eruptions: Regional Eczemas  Localized eczema can be a manifestation of AD, contact dermatitis (allergic/irritant), or other conditions. Ear Eczema (Otitis Externa):  Affects the external auditory canal, helix, or postauricular fold.  Often a sign of seborrheic dermatitis or allergic contact dermatitis (e.g., to neomycin in ear drops, nickel in earrings).  Secondary bacterial infection is common. Page 6 of 9 Ear eczema Eyelid Dermatitis:  Most often related to AD or allergic contact dermatitis.  Common allergens include fragrances, preservatives in cosmetics/eye drops, metals (nickel), and nail polish (transferred by hands).  Management requires identifying and eliminating triggers; patch testing is recommended. Breast (Nipple) Eczema:  Affects the areolae, often with oozing, crusting, and painful fissuring.  Can be the sole manifestation of AD in adult women, especially during breastfeeding.  Important: Unilateral nipple eczema persisting >3 months requires a biopsy to rule out Paget disease of the breast. Breast eczema Page 7 of 9 Hand Eczema:  Very common, especially in atopic individuals and certain occupations ("wet work" like healthcare, hairdressing).  Can be irritant, allergic, or atopic in origin.  Presents in various forms: vesicular ("dyshidrosis"), hyperkeratotic (thickened, fissured), or affecting fingertips (pulpitis). Hand eczema Page 8 of 9 Diaper (Napkin) Dermatitis:  An irritant dermatitis from prolonged contact with urine and feces, leading to maceration and skin breakdown.  Clinical Pearl: Typically spares the skin folds, unlike candidiasis or inverse psoriasis.

text: بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم LEPROSY Leprosy Chronic infectious disease caused by the Mycobacterium leprae bacilli with predilection for peripheral nerves and the skin In Egypt , leprosy is endemic in Assiout,Meniya and Sohag Leprosy can occur at all ages with peaks in those aged 10-14 and in those aged 35-44 years Causative organism The bacillus M. leprae is a very small, slightly curved acid-fast rod. that lives within cells, particularly macrophages and Schwann cells. Mycobacterium leprae has a complex cell wall composed of lipids, carbohydrates and proteins The bacillus requires a temperature of ~35°C to grow, and thus has a preference for cooler regions of the body (e.g. the nose, testicles and ear lobes) as well as regions where the peripheral nerves are close to the skin It cannot grow on artificial media ,but it can be cultivated in mice footpads and in armadillo. Mode of transmission  Droplet infection: Nasal discharge from untreated LL patients is the main source of infection in the community  An average incubation time of 5 years The clinical-immunologic spectrum of leprosy  It depends upon the level of specific cell-mediated immunity against M.Lepra which is genetically determined :  Tuberculoid: in patients with intact cell-mediated immunity  Lepromatous: in patients with depressed cell-mediated immunity  three types of borderline leprosy in between: borderline lepromatous ,borderline-borderline and borderline tuberculoid The WHO classification of leprosy  classification is based on the number of skin lesions:  single-lesion paucibacillary leprosy  paucibacillary leprosy (2-5 skin lesions)  multibacillary leprosy (more than 5 skin lesions). Clinical picture:  tuberculoid leprosy:  The lesions are limited to nerves and skin  cutaneous lesions : single or few well defined erythematous or hypopigmented plaques , The borders of the skin lesions are often slightly elevated  The cutaneous lesions have impaired sensation and devoid of hair and do not sweat Clinical picture:  tuberculoid leprosy:  Peripheral nerve affection: unilateral and/ or asymmetrical occuring early in the disease  there is thickening and tenderness of the peripheral nerves with pain ,paresthesia ,muscular weakness or paralysis  sometimes only neural involvement is present (neural leprosy) Clinical picture:  Lepromatous leprosy:  It is characterized by multiple, erythematous nodules and plaques.  Lesions are widespread, and symmetric in distribution Clinical picture:  Lepromatous leprosy:  bilateral infiltration of the earlobes  Infiltration of the skin of the forehead can lead to a leonine face  madarosis  Icthyosis of the skin of legs Clinical picture:  Lepromatous leprosy:  Peripheral nerve affection: bilateral and symmetrical occuring late in the disease , Anesthesia in a stocking or glove distribution may be seen, muscle wasting and atrophy, neurotrophic ulcers,bone resorption and loss of digits  nasal bleeding , saddle nose  Hoarseness of voice (laryngeal mucosa)  keratitis and corneal ulcers.  orchitis.  Lymphadenopathy and hepatomegaly Clinical picture:  Borderline leprosy:  The features are intermediate between the two ends of the spectrum  cutaneous lesions : few or several asymmetrical erythematous partly well defined plaques which usually have annular appearance  Peripheral nerve affection: several and asymmetrical Reactional states in leprosy:  Type 1 lepra Reaction :  An acute inflammatory response, often seen in borderline forms of leprosy, that affects existing skin lesions and nerves.  It is a delayed type hypersensitivity reaction  upgrading(reversal ) reaction  Skin lesions become red, swollen, and may ulcerate.  Inflammation of nerves (neuritis), which can lead to a sudden loss of sensory or motor function if not treated quickly.  Edema (swelling) of the hands, feet can occur. Reactional states in leprosy:  Type 2 lepra Reaction :(erythema nodosum leprosum)  A systemic immune-complex vasculitis that affects the skin and other organs in lepromatous and borderline lepromatous forms of leprosy.  painful, red nodules on the skin, often appearing on the arms, legs, and face.  Systemic symptoms like fever, malaise, and joint pain are common.  Can also involve nerve inflammation and damage.  There may be nephritis, iridocyclitis or orchitis Investigations  Slit skin smear :  mainly from the earlobes  To avoid bleeding, a fold of skin is firmly squeezed between the finger and thumb of the examiner and a small incision is made with a scalpel blade. The liquid obtained is smeared onto a slide and allowed to dry. The smear is usually stained by the Fite (or Ziehl-Neelsen) method and a search is made for red rods (against a blue background) Investigations  Skin biopsy :  tuberculoid leprosy :  dermal epitheliod granulomatous infiltrate is seen that have a linear pattern as it follows the course of a nerve.  Epithelioid histiocytes and Langhans giant cells are surrounded by lymphocytes.  The granulomas surrounds the fragmented nerve fibers  there is an absence of organisms, even with special stains.

text: LASERS in Dermatology Tattoo and pigment lasers Light-tissue interaction Melanosomes are melanin-containing organelles that range from ~0.3–1 micron in size, and they can act as a primary target for selective photothermolysis of pigmented lesions. Melanin has a broad absorption spectrum, which lends itself to possible targeting by a wide range of lasers. When the fluence threshold for melanosome disruption is reached, the melanin-containing cell dies. Treatment of tattoos with Q-switched nanosecond or picosecond lasers fragments the ink particles and selectively kills pigment containing cells, with resultant ink particle release. Subsequent removal of tattoo ink particles can occur via an epidermal crust and/or lymphatic transport while some particles are rephagocytosed by dermal cells. Examples of indications: tattoos, epidermal lesions as freckles, café au lait macules and dermal melanocytosis as nevi of ota , drug induced pigmentation. Q-switched ruby (694 nm), alexandrite (755 nm) and diode (810 nm) lasers, Q-switched Nd:YAG (1064 nm) laser and Q-switched frequency doubled Nd:YAG (532 nm) laser. Hair reduction lasers Light is probably absorbed by melanin in the hair shaft and matrix but it is likely that heat is then transferred to the true target structures, stem cells (mainly in the bulge area of the outer root sheath) and possibly blood vessels in the papilla. Photothermal ablation in the treatment of skin disorders SLOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to Describe principles, indications of vascular lasers Describe principles, indications of pigment lasers Describe principles, indications of hair reduction lasers Describe principles, indications of ablative lasers 1. Incisional with haemostasis. The CO2 laser (10 600 nm) can be used as an incisional or resurfacing instrument. Tissue can be incised by using a high-power, focused beam that vaporizes the tissue in its immediate path. 2. Ablative laser resurfacing. This was performed initially with scanned CO2 lasers, the immediate effect of which is ablation (or vaporization) of the epidermis and sometimes the superficial papillary dermis. Non-ablative and fractional modalities The prolonged healing times and side effects associated with ablative laser systems have led to the introduction of non-ablative and fractional non-ablative techniques. Non-ablative resurfacing. The aim of treatment is to selectively wound the upper dermis in order to induce dermal collagen remodelling. Examples; A variety of lasers (1064 and 1320 nmNd:YAG , 1450 nm diode and 1540 nm erbium glass lasers). Non-ablative facial rejuvenation for the treatment of fine lines and non-dynamic wrinkles. Fractional non-ablative resurfacing. This refers to the creation of microscopic treatment zones of coagulative damage to the epidermis and upper dermis. Clinical applications of fractional lasers include treatment of photoaging, striae distensae , and scars. Cutaneous laser surgery is a continually evolving area of dermatology. Development of new lasers, as well as improvements in existing lasers, continues to advance the field. “Laser” is an acronym for L ight A mplification by S timulated E mission of R adiation. Compared with other light sources, laser light is defined as monochromatic (i.e., a single wavelength), collimated (i.e., nondivergent), and coherent (i.e., in phase, with peaks and troughs of the light all aligned). Laser tissue interaction Light can interact with incident targets in one of several ways: reflected, transmitted, scattered, or absorbed. When reflected, transmitted, or scattered, the light has no effect on the target tissue. When absorbed, however, the light energy is transformed into heat. In most cases of laser therapy, it is the heat generated by absorption that produces the desired therapeutic effect. The concept of selective photothermolysis , originally promoted is the basis for all laser-tissue interactions. “A particular target chromophore absorbs light and is selectively damaged or destroyed.” The endogenous chromophores of importance are melanin, haemoglobin, water and collagen . Lasers are usually named after the constituents of the active or gain medium, which may be a gas, liquid, solid or semiconductor. The active medium is contained within an optical cavity. In its simplest form the optical cavity consists of two opposing mirrors, one of which is fully reflective and the other, the output coupler, is partly transparent. Photons moving parallel to the axis of the optical cavity are reflected between the two mirrors, in turn eliciting stimulated emission in the same axis. The energy required for the process of light amplification is supplied by an external source such as an electric current (if the active medium is a gas) or by a light source (flash lamp or other laser. This supply of energy is called optical pumping and amplifies the light until it is emitted through the output coupler. It then enters a delivery system that transmits it to the operator hand-piece. text: Urticaria & angioedema Definition Urticaria is a reactive skin disease to various allergic and non allergic stimuli characterized by rapid appearance of wheals and/or angioedema. Wheals:  well-demarcated pink or pale swelling of the superficial dermis surrounded by a red flare initially Wheals can range from very small, just a few millimeters, to much larger patches that can be several centimeters Pruritic (rubbing in nature) Fleeting nature, transient , individual lesions come and go rapidly (less than 24 hours) Wheal Pathogenesis The mast cell is the primary effector cell of urticaria Mast cell granules contain preformed mediators of inflammation Histamine is the most important mediator of urticaria It causes vasodilatation and increases vascular permeability leading to leakage of plasma and plasma proteins with the end results of tissue oedema and wheal formation Pathogenesis immunological : type I allergic reaction ( IgE mediated) Autoimmune (autoantibodies against IgE or its receptor on the surface of mast cell) in chronic autoimmune urticaria type I allergic reaction ( IgE mediated) Autoimmune Pathogenesis non immunological : direct mast cell degranulation :NSAIDs Food containing high levels of histamines : strawberries, tomatoes, shrimp. Classification Ordinary urticaria : Acute ( less than 6 weeks of continuous activity) Chronic ( 6 weeks or more of continuous activity "at least twice a week off treatment" ) chronic urticaria may be spontaneous or inducible (physical) Urticarial vasculitis Papular urticaria angioedema . Chronic autoimmune urticaria (autoantibodies against IgE or its receptor on the surface of mast cell) may be associated with other autoimmune conditions, most commonly thyroid disease (e.g., Hashimoto's thyroiditis), and rarely with chronic infections ( e.g helicobacter pylori infection). Chronic autoimmune urticaria is detected by autologus serum skin test (ASST) CSU with an unknown cause: chronic idiopathic urticaria (CIU), have no identifiable cause, even after a thorough medical history and testing Autologous serum skin test chronic inducible urticaria Inducible urticaria is characterized by definite and specific triggers of the development of wheals, angioedema, or both. cold contact urticaria : cold objects , air, fluids Heat contact urticaria : localized heat Dermographic urticarial (symptomatic dermographism) : linear wheals in response to mechanical shearing force ,develops within 5-10 minutes of stroking of the skin and persist for 15-30 minutes
