or longer. aquagenic urticaria: water of any temprature Solar urticaria : ultraviolet and or visible light Contact urticaria : contact of the skin with grass, animals , food , latex cholinergic urticaria : Multiple transient papular wheals 2-3 mm surrounded by obvious flare mainly on the trunk Pricky sensation Eliciting factors are sweat inducing stimuli ( physical exercise ,hot baths, sudden emotional stress ,spicy food ,alcohol Urticarial vasculitis It is characterized by cutaneous lesions resemble urticaria clinically but differ in : Longer lived ( individual lesions persist for>24 hours) Burning sensation , painful as well as pruritic Bluish red or cyanotic, more infiltrating leaves residual purpura and hyperpigmentation Associated features : fever,malaise,myalgia,arthralgia Idiopathic or associated with SLE ,hepatitis C, drug May be associated with systemic organ involvement ( renal,gastrointestinal,others) Urticarial vasculitis name: Drug reactions & dermatologic emergencies
text: Drug Reactions & Dermatological Emergencies SLOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to Know the principles of diagnosing and managing patients with the following presentations, including referral to appropriate specialties: • Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome • Erythroderma • Necrotising fasciitis • Meningococcemia • Angioedema • Generalised pustular psoriasis • Drug reactions including erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis spectrum Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (SSSS) Toxin-mediated disease caused by Staphylococcus aureus exotoxins, leading to rapid generalized red skin, peeling, fever, hypotension, and potential multi-organ failure. Clinical Picture • Prodrome: 2–3 days of malaise, fever, chills, nausea, and abdominal pain. • Rash: Diffuse red rash spreading from the trunk to the palms and soles. • Blisters & Peeling: Large, flaccid, sterile blisters form and rupture easily, peeling off in sheets (desquamation) to leave raw, burn-like skin. • Nikolsky Sign: Positive (gentle pressure causes skin to separate). • Systemic Complications: Arrhythmias, liver/kidney failure, DIC, and acute respiratory distress. Figure 1 – Diffuse erythematous rash and peeling of the skin in SSSS. Management • Aggressive supportive care (fluids/pressure support for hypotension) and removal of inciting factors. • Obtain cultures, then start a β-lactamase–resistant anti-staphylococcal antibiotic. Erythroderma Generalized red, scaly skin eruption involving >90% of the body surface. Etiology • Idiopathic, or secondary to underlying conditions: eczema, psoriasis, drug reactions (e.g., allopurinol, calcium-channel blockers, anticonvulsants, lithium), cutaneous T-cell lymphoma/leukemia, or dermatomyositis. Clinical Picture • Symptoms: Severe itching (pruritus) is typically first, followed by fever and malaise. • Complications: Heat, fluid, and protein loss across the skin can cause severe hypotension, electrolyte imbalances, heart failure, and death. Figure 2 - Erythroderma Management • Hospitalization and supportive care (hydration, nutrition, monitoring, temperature control). • Stop any suspect medications and perform skin biopsies if needed. • Topical corticosteroids, emollients, compresses, and antihistamines for itch; antibiotics if infected. Necrotizing Fasciitis A rapidly spreading, deep skin infection causing subcutaneous tissue death (necrosis). Classification & Risk Factors • Type I (Polymicrobial): Mixed aerobic and anaerobic bacteria; common in immunocompromised or diabetic patients. • Type II (Monomicrobial): Typically Streptococcus pyogenes or Staphylococcus aureus; often follows trauma in healthy individuals. • Risk Factors: Diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, immunosuppression, or minor skin injuries/surgeries. Clinical Picture • Early diffuse swelling, developing into dark red/burgundy bullae and frank gangrene. • Severe pain (out of proportion), severe swelling (indurated edema), gas under the skin (crepitation), muscle weakness, and foul-smelling discharge. • Rapidly leads to sepsis, shock, and organ failure. Figure 3 – Necrotizing fasciitis Management • Emergency surgical debridement of necrotic tissue and aggressive sepsis management. • Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (or targeted anti-streptococcal therapy). Meningococcemia A life-threatening bloodstream infection caused by Neisseria meningitidis, spread via respiratory droplets. Peak incidence is in infants (6–12 months). Clinical Picture • Sudden onset of flu-like symptoms (fever, chills, malaise) with a red spotted (maculopapular/petechial) rash. • Rapidly progresses over hours to severe purple spots (purpura), DIC, shock, and death. Figure 4 – Meningococcemia petechial rash Management • Emergency medical priority: Obtain blood cultures and start IV antibiotics immediately. • First-line Antibiotics: 3rd-generation cephalosporin (e.g., ceftriaxone) or IV Penicillin G (Chloramphenicol if allergic). Angioedema Localized, non-pitting swelling of the deep skin, GI tract, or airways due to increased vascular permeability. Etiology • Triggers: Idiopathic, foods/allergens, physical agents, or drugs (ACE inhibitors in 10%–25% of cases; penicillins, NSAIDs). • C1 Esterase Inhibitor Deficiency: Hereditary (autosomal dominant) or acquired. Clinical Picture • Acute swelling of face, lips, tongue, extremities, or genitalia. • Often non-pruritic, burning swelling; may occur with hives (urticaria) in 50% of cases. • Airway Compromise: Upper airway involvement can lead to fatal asphyxiation. Figure 5 - Angioedema Management • Airway First: Secure airway immediately (intubation/ICU) if there is hoarseness or difficulty breathing. • Allergic/Histamine-Mediated: Epinephrine (for severe cases/shock), H1/H2 antihistamines, and corticosteroids. Generalized Pustular Psoriasis (GPP) A rare, life-threatening variant of psoriasis linked to IL-36 pathway dysfunction (IL36RN mutations). Triggers • Withdrawal of systemic steroids, acute infections, stress, hypocalcemia, or pregnancy. Clinical Picture • Cutaneous: Rapid onset of painful, 2–3 mm sterile pustules on red skin that merge into 'lakes of pus', drying into scabs and peeling. • Systemic Symptoms: High fever, chills, severe skin pain, exhaustion, headache, nausea, rapid heart rate, low blood pressure, and risk of organ failure. Figure 6 – Generalized pustular psoriasis Management • Systemic psoriasis medications and supportive care. • Targeted Biologic: Spesolimab (IL-36 receptor monoclonal antibody). Erythema Multiforme (EM) An acute, self-limited Type IV hypersensitivity reaction. Etiology • 50% idiopathic. • Infections (Most Common): Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV 1 & 2), Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and other viral/bacterial infections. • Drugs: Sulfa drugs (30%), antibiotics, anticonvulsants, NSAIDs. Clinical Picture • Classic Target Lesion: <3 cm, round, regular border with ≥3 concentric zones (dark/blistered center surrounded by lighter ring and red border). Typically on hands, forearms, face, and trunk. • EM Minor: Typical targets/papules on extremities with minimal or no mucosal involvement. • EM Major: Target lesions with severe, painful mucosal blisters/erosions (lips, mouth, eyes, genitals) and systemic symptoms (fever, fatigue). Figure 7 – Target lesions, iris lesions, mucous membrane erosions in erythema multiforme Management • Mild: Symptomatic care, mouthwashes, topical steroids, and soft/liquid diet. • Severe: Consider oral steroids (e.g., Prednisone). • Recurrent HSV-EM: Continuous prophylactic antiviral therapy (e.g., Acyclovir). Stevens–Johnson Syndrome (SJS) & Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN) Severe, life-threatening, drug-induced mucocutaneous reactions causing massive keratinocyte death and epidermal detachment ('scalded skin'). Clinical Picture • Prodrome: Fever, stinging eyes, and painful swallowing (1–3 days before rash). • Skin Lesions: Dusky red/purpuric macules starting on trunk/face, turning gray as skin dies, forming flaccid blisters that detach easily. • Signs: Positive Nikolsky sign and Asboe–Hansen sign (blisters extend laterally with pressure). • Mucosa: Severe painful erosions in >90% of cases (mouth, eyes, genitalia). Classification by Body Surface Area (BSA) Detachment • SJS: <10% BSA detachment. • SJS/TEN Overlap: 10%–30% BSA detachment. • TEN: >30% BSA detachment. Figure 8 – Stevens Johnson syndrome Histopathology • Early: Scattered apoptotic keratinocytes. • Late: Subepidermal blister with full-thickness epidermal necrosis. Management • Crucial First Step: Immediately identify and stop the culprit drug. • Transfer to Burn Unit or ICU if BSA detachment is ≥10%. • Burn-like supportive care (hydration, wound care with Vaseline gauze, eye care). • Systemic therapies may include IVIg, cyclosporine, TNF inhibitors, or steroids. References • 1. James WD, Elston DM, Treat JR, Rosenbach MA, Neuhaus IM. Andrews’ Diseases of the Skin: Clinical Dermatology. 14th ed. Philadelphia: Elsevier; 2025.
